The hon. member showed me this newspaper paragraph just as I was coming into the chamber, and I could hardly credit that a gentleman in Mr. Drew's position would make such a statement. His statement is a direct reflection upon the department over which I have the honour to preside. It has to do with the matter of depriving the men of the reserve army of their votes. It is exactly on a par with what has already been discussed. I only want to say that nothing has been done, that no communication has been had with Colonel Drew with regard to his statement because I have not regarded it as necessary. Public opinion perhaps will be the best answer in that respect, after the announcement I made yesterday concerning the arrangements which had been made for the reserve army to vote.
It happens that one camp in the whole of Ontario had been fixed for a certain date before the date of the Ontario election was known. There have been screams from several quarters, not in this house, and not by men of the reserve army, to the effect that the Department of National Defence had deprived men who were going to that camp of their votes. I think "disfranchise" was one word used and "iniquitous" was another. It does seem to me, after the statement I made yesterday, that hon. members and the public generally and public men like Mr. Drew might accept the fact that we are doing everything we possibly can to make provision so that these men can vote, even curtailing the camp, as I explained yesterday, in order that they may get home in time. Has the previous item passed? The other evening we were discussing alternative service work camps, and there is a further question I should like to ask in this regard. I understand that about a thousand conscientious objectors were moved from the prairies to British Columbia under some arrangement with the provincial government to do forestry work. The report I have is dated April 2il, 1943, and I understand these men were to be paid fifty cents per day for the work they did, while the forestry department was to be paid an allowance of $2.50 per day for their board and keep. Are these people still there under this arrangement?- because it seems to me they could render more essential service at this time if they were back on the prairies. I mean right to-day. As I pointed out the other night, there is a shortage of man-power for haying; within a few days the harvest season will be here, and without manpower our farmers cannot take off the large harvest we expect in western Canada. speakeroldname: Hon. T. A. CRERAR (Minister of Mines and Resources):
speechtext:
The item we are consider-
5230	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Mines and Resources
mg is No. 12, and the question asked by my friend refers I think to a previous item already passed.
It was under discussion when the committee rose.

I understood that the item passed at that time, but I have no objection to answering, and this explanation is perhaps necessary. Alternate service is carried on under two different branches of the department. Part of it is under the national parks administration and part under the surveys and engineering branch. The conscientious [DOT]objectors who were sent to British Columbia over a year ago were sent to do forest protection work. There was a fear, how well justified I cannot say, that incendiary bombs might be dropped on British Columbia forests, as I believe did happen in some of the forests in the Pacific states. It was considered that the protection of the forests against a hazard *of that kind was more important than the work that conscientious objectors were doing at that time in the national parks, and they were accordingly sent to British Columbia, to the number of some six or seven hundred.
I think the arrangement called for one thousand, and that seven hundred were sent out.

Between six and seven
hundred men were ultimately sent. Some of them have been brought back and placed at other work, largely upon farms because in the past year that policy has been adopted. A few more than four hundred of these conscientious objectors are still in British Columbia, and I am advised that they are cutting cordwood for fuel needs next winter.

This item permits I think of a discussion of a problem vitally important to the war effort of this nation which arises directly out of an order published to-day in regard to an increase in the price of newsprint. In my opinion the best use is not being made of the services of conscientious objectors in the production of firewood and of pit-props. I would not bring this matter up now were it not that there is no more important factor in the war effort of this nation than the production of pulpwood out of which paper and paper products are made. There is such a shortage of man-power in the production of wood pulp that during the past year one million cords less were produced in Canada than the production required to meet present day needs, the demands of the United States, Great Britain and other countries of the empire.

This matter comes under the department administration by the minister in that one of the branches with which he is concerned is forest products laboratories, to which reference was made the other day. I know the interest of the Minister in the development of our resources and in ensuring that they shall be utilized to the achievement of the greatest possible war effort on the part of this nation. That requires man-power to be properly allocated to the production of pulpwood, which is one of the greatest industries in this country.
I take this matter up at this time because of its transcendent importance in the relationship of the publishers of the United States of America towards the war effort of this dominion. There has been during recent weeks a pronounced antagonism on the part of the American publishers towards the restriction that has taken place in this country in the production of necessary pulpwood. I find this, and I am sure that the minister is aware that it exists, that a feeling is springing up in the United States that we in Canada in raising the price of pulpwood and in not assuring the full production that is needed by the United States are actually trying to take some advantage of the United States, whose main importations of this product come from Canada. This morning the press carried this notification:
Ottawa, July 21.-The prices board announced to-night that effective next September 1 the ceiling on newsprint in Canada will be raised $4 a ton to conform with an increase of the same amount being put in effect in the United States.
The announcement was made jointly in Ottawa and Washington.
It said that on the basis of cost figures the prices board "is of the opinion that the present proposed increase is inadequate and that further discussions with the American authorities will need to be held."
There was an increase on March 1 of $4 a ton and there is a further increase now of S4 a ton. I sum up the situation as far as the necessity for pulp production in Canada is concerned. Lack of sufficient man-power during last season has resulted in the shortage to which I have already referred of one million cords of pulpwood. Vital war production has been endangered, because paper and pulpwood occupy to-day a position which is unequalled by any other industry in the war effort of the nation. Essential foreign exchange is being sacrificed, and as I have already mentioned, publishers in the United States are becoming antagonized against Canada. This is so important that it requires the very best consideration which the minister and

War Appropriation-Mines and Resources
the other members of the cabinet can give to it. I have before me the American Newspaper Publishers' Association bulletin of July 12, 1943, ' of which I shall read excerpts to place before the house and the country the serious situation in which we shall find ourselves unless we do something to assure that United States publishers receive from this country supplies of pulpwood necessary for paper production. This is what it says:
Regardless of the facts as they are interpreted to various publishers, it does seem that the matter of price is interwoven with the matter of supply from Canada. The Canadians have stated that they will continue to supply newsprint to the United States at the rate of 210,000 tons per month through the third quarter, but they do not indicate in any way what they will do in the fourth quarter. There have been suggestions that the Canadians will reduce the tonnage going to the United States from 210,000 tons in the fourth quarter regardless of what price prevails.
This is the magazine of the publishers' association, distributed for the information of the papers of the United States, and if this idea is allowed to be broadcast, the value of the work of our war information branch in the United States will be greatly reduced, if not nullified. The bulletin goes on:
On the present basis Canadian mills are delivering 210.000 tons to the United States each month, 16,000 tons to Canadian consumers, and 20,000 tons are provided for overseas, making a total of 246,000 tons.
I particularly direct attention to the next paragraph, which indicates the seriousness of this matter, having regard to the importance of this industry and the necessity of retaining the good feeling of the press of the United States:
There are a considerable number of publishers who recognize that the wood supply is the key to newsprint production in Canada but back of the wood supply is the man-power situation. These publishers feel that if sufficient man-power is provided in Canada there can be a reasonably adequate supply of newsprint, but the supply from Canada will diminish unless Canada takes steps to assure a greater wood cut.
I repeat to the minister how important it is for his department, charged with the administration of the resources of this dominion, that this matter receive the serious attention which I am sure he will give it in order that the possibility of ill-feeling being engendered between these two nations shall be avoided.
While United States publishers recognize that it is Canada's own responsibility to fix her man-power policies and execute her war programme, disquieting reports continue to reach United States publishers about a considerable amount of man-power being taken from cutting wood into army service, but these forces, by Canadian law, cannot be sent overseas except on a volunteer basis. In addition, in Canada
agriculture or farming is a basis for deferment from military service but pulpwood cutting is not classified as a basis for deferment from military service. In the United States both pulpwood cutting and agriculture are grounds for deferment from military service.
If the policy is pursued by the Canadians of not taking any special steps to maintain volume because of the man-power situation and the supply of newsprint from Canada to the United States is allowed to dwindle it can be seen that the Canadians will be making frequent and periodical visits to Washington^ demanding further increases in newsprint prices.
That is a strong condemnation of what these publishers believe Canada is going to do, that is, continue to secure rises in the price while not assuring the necessary production.
After all, the volume of production in any business as in newsprint has an important bearing upon cost. If the price of newsprint is to be maintained at a level which will make it possible for American newspapers to operate without losses aud have some assurance and security about their supply of newsprint then there must be clarification soon about what Canada will do in assuring a supply of newsprint commensurate with the needs of American newspapers.
That indicates how serious the matter is- that these publishers in the United States who require Canadian production believe or suggest that in continuing to raise the price without having the necessary man-power to assure the production they require, we are taking advantage of them at this time.
I need not point out to the minister how important the pulpwood industry is to Canada. If a feeling of this kind is allowed to develop among publishers in the United States, the adverse effect on the joint effort of these two nations in the war can well be imagined.
As late as 1940 Canada was producing more than fifty per cent of the world output. Our domestic consumption does not amount to very much, but the United States consumption constitutes the major demand for our pulp-forest products. So important, however-I again accentuate this

is the pulp and paper industry in this country that the Dominion Bureau of Statistics has said:

When foreign exchange is so important-considering the problem from that angle alone-a very special effort should be made on the part of our country to ensure that this shortage in the production of pulp, -which directly affects the supply of newsprint, shall not be permitted to continue.
According to the United States Department -of Commerce, forestry branch, the army and navy and essential civilian needs will require this year 15,000,000 tons of paper and pulp-wood. It will take two and a quarter million -cords of pulpwood to manufacture the paper needed in the United States in 1943 to package food supplies and munitions for overseas shipment, and enormous quantities of pulpwood will be needed for the manufacture of smokeless powder, plastics and many other products that are indicated.
All this adds up to the point I have been endeavouring to make, that with the shortage in man-power which resulted in such a material reduction in production in Canada last year, *every available man that can be placed in the industry now should be assigned to it. Recently a survey was made to ascertain the situation and it was found by one of the companies that *only 36-9 per cent of the minimum requirements of men were in the bush during the week of July 2. It is impossible to secure the necessary man-power as the situation is to-day. In the United States the production of pulpwood is regarded as of great importance. One of the chief reasons for the reduction in Canadian production has been that while farmers are allowed to go into the woods and work for sixty days in any year, so long as employment does not interfere with agricultural production, during the past few months there has been a
[DOT]	grave fear among farmers-the proportion being two in the province of Quebec to one in Ontario-who ordinarily go into the bush during the winter to look after the cutting, that they will lose their rights to postponement by so doing, and the result is that they stay at home during the winter or other slack season. The situation will become even more serious unless action is taken immediately to put men to work in the woods. Entirely apart from the regular demand for wood fibre, the
[DOT]	demand is increasing in war production, and as shipping space becomes freer, more paper will be needed for export, even though Britain to-day is reduced to 20 per cent of the prewar level. Already the allied nations are .piling up reserves of paper to send to the

countries that are at present occupied, looking to the time when they will be relieved of the axis invaders and occupants, so as to make the free publication of world news possible in order to benefit the people of those countries by restoring them a free press.
It is essential to the war effort that the United States, Britain land the other countries I have mentioned should have sufficient paper to print the news to strengthen public morale. Five thousand tons of newsprint were recently shipped from Canada to the near east and North Africa for the very purpose I have mentioned. First, we must not lose this valuable trade by our failure to make the necessary man-power available for the purpose, even though it is part-time work and agricultural workers are freed for the purpose. Second, we must look ahead to the post-war period so that this industry shall not be permitted to fall into the position where the United States, our main customer, taking 71 per cent of our production, may turn to other methods in order to supply those needs now filled by pulpwood. More important than anything else-and it is on this basis that I make this appeal-we must not allow American publishers and the American newspaper association to get the idea that we in Canada are trying to take advantage of them in the matter of price. If we do, we may have an adverse press in the United States, and a press that is adverse in the slightest degree, a press that adopts an attitude antagonistic to Canada's war effort, resulting in a tendency to separate us one from the other in our united effort and to arouse suspicions between nations engaged in the common crusade, should be averted no matter what course must be taken in order to avoid it.
I appreciate the opportunity which the committee has given me to place this matter before hon. members in this sketchy manner. I have not desired to take up time with statistics, but I press the point strongly. We must not, we dare not, allow the attitude that is set forth in that publishers' association pamphlet to become general. There is only one way to avoid it, and that is by a proper allocation of necessary man-power. The attitude of American publishers is important to the war effort of this dominion. It is more important than we here can estimate. This is a matter that deserves, I submit, the most serious consideration of the minister and of the government. Once lost, the favour of the American publishers, their appreciation of what we are doing in Canada, will be very hard to regain.

War Appropiiation-Mines and Resources

I am glad to see an awakened interest in the lands, forests and parks branch of the department. For the past five or six years we have not been giving sufficient attention to all that is involved in this item. When these matters came up on previous occasions there was little discussion. There was little more than ten or fifteen minutes of discussion last session on the whole item. May I point out a grave mistake which the government may make in regard to this very important asset. I refer to the natural resources of the north-west territories as far as the Yukon.
The government must consider seriously the activities that are taking place in the great development now under way in that country as a result of the work on the Alaska highway. A large number of Americans have come there and they are interested in the project from the military standpoint, but there is also the postwar importance of the matter to be considered. Our soldiers are now overseas and this territory will be in the future one of the greatest sources of employment and development in Canada. Many of our young soldiers are graduates of our universities in electrical engineering and in various other branches of that great profession. A great many of the young men who are now in Sicily and Africa used to go into this territory in the summer when they were students. The government must not be unmindful of the importance of this to our engineering graduates in the days to come. In dealing with these properties they must not lose sight of that.
In my opinion these various branches of the lands, forests and parks branch of this department will be of great service to Canada, or at any rate they can be made of great service to Canada after the war. Do not forget that these great natural resources of all kinds are going to be a great source of employment for our soldiers after this war; and above all, do not make the mistake that was made in Ontario with the natural resources of that province. From the Ottawa river right through Nipigon, some years ago, financial men came from New York and other places and grabbed the whole territory, the timber, water powers, mines, forests and great natural resources of new Ontario, with the result that valuable resources of various kinds there went for a song. Our mines and their wealth and everything else were underwritten and have been given away for a song, and now we are going to make the same fatal mistake in these great western areas if we are not careful, in regard to the north-west territories and the Yukon. Canada is not going to be
any land of milk and honey after the war is over; it is not going to be an easy place in which to live. Those hon. members who wish to do so may go home; this opposition does not consist of only one or two or three hon. members, as a section of the press apparently thinks. There are others here who have taken part in these debates on this item last year all alone, when no one else would do so. This is going to be a desperately poor country after the war. As I say, our natural resources have been given away and frittered away at a rapid rate; you have only to look at the export figures in regard to lumber, timber, mines and pulpwood and everything else which the axis powers have bought to make munitions to be used against our own men, to see how this is done. I say no part of the public domain, whether it is the timber, the soil or the minerals, should be given away in any haphazard way. It is all very well for people to come here from other countries and help develop our resources and water powers, to supply capital and all that sort of thing; our policy in that regard, has been commendable all along the line, but the government should be very careful in what it does with the great assets we have in our natural resources, and use them to develop Canada and aid our empire.
I am surprised at some of the things that have been done this session in the name of the war, things which are not relevant to the war at all. It seems to me the work of this whole department is devoted to only one part of Canada and that Ontario has been given little or nothing in national parks, forests or aid in streams, as was shown last year in the debate on this very item. We are forgotten year after year on this item. In the way this matter has been dealt with by order in council, private negotiations and private contracts over the head of parliament I see signs of the same mistake that was made in new Ontario. I agree with the policy of permitting those with capital to help develop this or any other territory. I do not agree with the policy of giving away our resources, nor do I agree with the way we have surrendered our sovereignty unregulated, to Americans, in this area. We are supposed to be a nation with status dreams, but I have been surprised at what has gone on in this department in connection with the giving away of property secretly, and by order in council, over the head of parliament to those who do not belong to this country. Money is needed and capital everywhere for development, but there is no real protection in giving away the sovereignty of the people of Canada
5234	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Mines and Resources
in regard to this property. I wish the miaister every success ia his work; ever siace I have been a member of the house I have endeavoured to help him by offering constructive criticisms, but I point out that these are our richest assets and they should not be further squandered in such a way. After the war all we will have left to fall back upon will be our natural resources, and in future we will have to be very careful to have no more barter or sale or squandering of those resources as we have had in the past.

The hon. member for Lake Centre expressed some concern over a possible shortage of newsprint, and I think, by inference at any rate, argued that the men employed under this vote should be sent to cut pulpwood rather than pit-props and cordwood. I think that is a fair inference to take from his remarks.
I do not think he said that in so many words, did he?

No, but the hon. member made reference to pit-props and cordwood and urged the importance of maintaining supplies of pulpwood; I think that is a fair statement. I do not take nearly as dark a view as my hon. friend does of the effect on American opinion of any shortage that may arise in connection with supplies of newsprint. I am aware that some agitation has been carried on in this connection by a few newspapers in the United States, but I think the great majority of newspapers in that country recognize the realities of the situation. I have not noticed, and I doubt if my hon. friend has noticed, any serious reduction in the size of newspapers published either in Canada or in the United States. In Great Britain, almost from the early days of the war, the newspapers were reduced in size by more than a half; some of them, I believe, carry only about a quarter of the news and views they carried formerly. After all, it is a question of man-power. You cannot put your hand in a hat and pull out man-power for coal mines, for transporting grain, to which the Minister of Trade and Commerce referred the other evening; for base metal mines, for the army, for the air force, for the navy and for all the multitude of things that require man-power to-day, including agriculture. There is no magic in getting these men.
But there might be a good plan.

Well, hon. gentlemen
opposite have talked about plans last year
Mr. Church.]
and this year, but so far as I am aware they have not at any time suggested any plan which might be adopted by the government. I can tell my hon. friend that if he can produce a plan it will receive the earnest consideration of the government.
We did not suggest any magic.
There has been a great deal of criticism. I do not object to that, but there have been no constructive suggestions as to how the problem might be solved.
My hon. friend has not been listening very closely to the debates, or he would not say that.

I suggest that the leader of the opposition read again his speeches and those of the members of his party, and see what he can extract from them in the way of constructive criticism. The other evening, on another vote, the hon. member for Lake Centre I thought argued that we should not keep these men at forestry work, and moved that the item be reduced to SI. He argued at that time, if I remember correctly, that there was a great scarcity of agricultural labour, and that these people should be sent to work on the farms. To-day the hon. gentleman comes forward with another suggestion, that -they should be taken from the work of cutting pit-props and cordwood and put to work cutting pulpwood. Well, I recognize the need for pulpwood, but I think it is far more important to ensure, as far as we can, adequate supplies of fuel for our people next winter. I think that is more important than putting men, who might be doing that work, at the job of cutting pulpwood so that the size of newspapers may be maintained, and I think that would be the judgment of the country.
Under this vote -I think I might make this explanation. The Department of Mines and Resources does not allocate these men. That is done now by the Department of Labour, under national selective service. When the problem with respect to conscientious objectors arose much earlier it was recognized, and 1 believe public opinion supported this view, that they should be put at useful work. Some of them were put to work in the parks. Others were put to work in building a section of the trans-Canada highway, in northern Ontario. That is connected with one of the votes we are now considering. They were given various tasks of that kind. But as the situation developed they were transferred from this work, much of which was considered not particularly essential, and put at more essen-

War Appropriation-Mines and Resources
tial work. A year ago they were sent to British Columbia for the purpose of building roads, lookout stations, and the general development of the fire protection service in the forests of British Columbia. Lately they have been sent to agricultural labour. Some of them, particularly in western Alberta, have been cutting pit-props for use in the mines. Generally speaking they have been doing useful work of that kind.
We were asked by the Department of Labour, and prior to that by the Department of National War Services, to supervise the work of a number of these men. So far as this vote was concerned, that was put under our surveys and engineering branch, and they were put to work building part of a section of the trans-Canada highway in northern Ontario. There were 202 engaged in that work at the end of February. That number has dwindled to practically nothing. I note here that 96 have been sent to the neighbour-, hood of Elmira, Ontario, for agricultural work, and 77 to the Chatham district. So that today there are no conscientious objectors engaged in road construction in northern Ontario. They have been sent to other work, in agriculture. That is the policy which has been followed generally.
It is quite possible that next winter we may have to provide work for a number of these conscientious objectors. Probably they will be employed in the cutting of cordwood, or whatever other useful work they can do. But I doubt if parliament would get much support from the country if we were to say that the cutting of pulpwood to maintain ordinary supplies of newsprint was more important than, for instance, getting out fuel, and that sort of thing.
The hon. member also made reference to the need for foreign exchange, and read an extract published by the bureau of statistics in 1940. There is no question that in 1940, particularly the early part of it, our exchange situation vis-a-vis the United States was one that gave some concern. But that picture has changed altogether and, as my hon. friend probably knows, for the last year or more the exchange problem with the United States has not given the government any worry at all. Indeed there was a time when we thought we were accumulating too much American exchange in Canada. I believe that was the result, largely, of war orders placed by the United States with Canadian factories. The work these conscientious objectors are now doing on farms in Ontario and elsewhere is of first importance.

No one has suggested that the men should not be utilized for the purpose of getting out firewood, or that that was not an important piece of work.
I have referred to the expenditure in connection with conscientious objectors, and it is one which runs into a tremendous amount of money. I would ask the minister this simple question: How many cords of wood did conscientious objectors get out in the last year? An answer to that question would tell whether or not this expenditure, running around a quarter of a million dollars, has been justified.

I cannot answer the hon. member's question offhand. I know that as to conscientious objectors under the direction of the Department of Mines and Resources we could get that information. I believe I am correct in saying, however, that there has been a considerable amount of cordwood cut in some of the national parks, for use next winter. However, if the hon. member wants the information I believe I can get an estimate for him.

The minister said this party had made no suggestions. I shall make one, in connection with this item for the cutting of wood. The first suggestion I make is that the government remove that part of the National Resources Mobilization Act limiting service to the western hemisphere. I do that for this reason. We are bound to see a further reduction-and in my opinion the reduction has not yet started-in the size of newspapers. As the man-power situation gets tighter, and it is bound to get tighter, we are going to see all our newspapers, particularly the big revenue-producing papers, like the Toronto Star Weekly, and the Sunday editions of American papers, greatly curtailed *because of a lack of newsprint. That is inevitable; I do not see how it can be avoided. It is like the invasion of Europe; it is one of the things which in my view is bound to happen. We need our pulpwood for direct war purposes. We need our cellulose for explosives. We are faced, as I see it with the problem of having to say to the American publishers, "I am sorry; we cannot supply you with newsprint." Then the American publishers will say to us, "Why have you a home defence army?" They will say, "You could supply us with newsprint if you did not have that army."

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
If I may be allowed to interject, the hon. member for Lake Centre thanked the committee for allowing him to make his statement this morning. I do not believe this discussion is in order. The manpower question was dealt with several times in the present session, and if the hon. member wishes to speak on that subject he will have an opportunity when we get into supply. I am sure the Minister of Mines and Resources cannot answer some of the questions put to him at the present time.
5236	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Mines and Resources

I am simply answering the Minister of Mines and Resources, who said that no suggestions with regard to man-power had been made from this side of the house. At this time, with a market for every ton of newsprint for advertising purposes, a market more profitable than ever existed before, in my opinion we in Canada are in an inferior position, an intolerable position, with regard to American journals, unless we can say, "We cannot supply you with this newsprint because every individual is doing his utmost, under the same conditions as your men are, to win the war." That is my suggestion and that is all I have to say to the minister.

Could the
minister give us some information with regard to this particular item? First, I should like the total number of men in these alternative service camps. I understand him to say that there were still 400 in British Columbia, but I should like to have the total for all Canada. Next, I should like to know if any of the men in these camps are doing work other than that of taking out fuel wood and cutting pit-props. I have in mind particularly whether any work is still being carried on in the national parks. In the correspondence I have had with the men in these camps there is no complaint that they are working too hard; there is no objection to that, but that they feel they are doing non-essential work. I have in mind that they are engaged, I believe, in putting in ski jumps or something of the sort in Banff national park, and in building roads in Prince Albert national park to attract tourist traffic. I agree with the minister that that sort of work is not very essential, and I think the committee will agree generally that these men should be doing more essential work.
I should like some information with respect ;o the wages and maintenance costs of these nen. I understood the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross) to say he was under the impression that the men were getting 50 cents a day as pay and $2.50 as maintenance.
I could hardly credit that, and I should like a statement from the minister. An amount of $2.50 a day seems amazing for maintenance only, as the army is able to maintain men for $1 or less per day. The lumber companies call for tenders for the board and lodging of their men, and it is usually recognized that this can be done for $1 or $1.25 a day. I think it is a disgrace that we should pay a man only 50 cents a day and then expect him to buy clothing, work gloves, work shoes, overalls and things of the kind which are necessary for this sort of work. If [The Chairman.]
these men are doing a proper day's work, and I assume they are-the government ought to see to it that they do a day's work- they should be paid more than 50 cents a day. If they are working in the field or in the lumber camps or for private concerns they would get much better pay than that. I do not want to see these men coddled, but I do want to see them given fair pay for a fair day's work and not be penalized because of any particular views they may hold.

My latest figures are for May 31. I wish to make it clear that these-are men in the lands, -parks and forest branch, of the Department of Mines and Resources. On May 31 there were 106 at Banff, 56 at Jasper and 82 at Kootenay. I think I am correct in saying that these men were mainly engaged in the cutting of pit-props and cordwood, although there was one lumbering operation, and of course lumber is a ' scarce commodity. In Prince Albert there were 11, and in Riding Mountain there were 35. I think the 35 men in Riding Mountain park were all engaged in cutting cordwood. Their remuneration is 50 cents per day, and there is an allowance of 56 cents a day for provisions, which I assume would cover board and lodging. There is an allowance of 6 cents a day for medical and dental services, and 71 cents a day for administration expenses, including supervision of camps and personnel and also repair of equipment and purchase of materials and supplies other than provisions, which would cover axes, saws and that sort of thing. For the period under review the total cost per man was $1.83 per day. Mr. Chairman, which item are we considering?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: We are taking together the three items covering alternative service work camps.

A moment ago I gave the number of the men in the surveys and engineering branch. The number of men employed on road work in northern Ontario as at February 28 was 202. I think almost without, exception these men have all been absorbed into agricultural labour; instead of working on the roads in northern Ontario, they are working on farms. They receive the same wages, 50 cents a day plus their keep. I have not the board and lodging expenses in this case. The straw boss, I assume, the man who looks after a group, also a conscientious objector, is paid 75 cents a day.

Am I to take it from the minister's remarks that all these men are either cutting pit-props or cordwood?

War Appropriation-Mines and Resources
I think that is correct. There may be some lumbering operations going on in one of the western parks.

How is the
cordwood disposed of? Is it sold to private companies for resale to the public, or does the government use it?
According to my information the cordwood is sold to municipalities and others under tender.

The minister did not answer the question I asked with respect to the wages paid these men. I do not know where you could hire labour in Canada for 50 cents a day. If these men are just out on a picnic, not doing much work, the government may feel that 50 cents a day is all right, but I cannot imagine that the government would go to the trouble of setting up these camps without seeing that they got a good day's work from the men. It seems to me that if we are facing up to the situation and saying to these men, " You must do some service for the state," a fair remuneration should be paid. If a man has certain views which he feels preclude him from doing military service, he ought to do some kind1 of service but he ought not to be penalized. We have no right to say to a man, " Under our constitution you have the right to hold certain views, but we reserve the right to punish you for having those views." If we are going to say to a man that he has a right to alternative service, then we have a responsibility to see that he is properly paid for that service.
When I was in Toronto some weeks ago I came across the case of a man who was a Quaker, a member of the Society of Friends. As the minister knows, for centuries these people have been averse to bearing arms. This man was married and he was to be sent to an alternative service camp and paid 50 cents a day. He had a family, and he just did not know what to do. In a case like that the government would be justified in paying -.a dependents' allowance to the man's wife. Does the government do that, and if not, why not? On what basis is this 50 cents a day being paid as a wage for the kind of work these men are doing?	.

This 50 cents a day
remuneration was decided upon when the administration of the conscientious objectors was under the Department of National War Services. When these men are called up, if they are able to make a case for themselves as conscientious objectors they are allowed to do alternative service work, as it is described in this vote. It is one of these matters in
which public opinion has an important bearing. If a young fellow proves to the tribunal that he is a conscientious objector and then you said to him, "You go and work on this job at $5 a day" there would be a great deal of criticism from the public. It is a question of arriving at what is fair and reasonable.
I cannot say definitely whether conscientious objectors who are working on the farm get higher pay than those who are working on government jobs, because, I repeat, the Department of Mines and Resources is simply the agent of another department of the government in supervising the work of a number of these men. When they leave us to go to agricultural labour we have no further supervision over them, and I cannot tell my hon. friend what scale of wages they receive when they are put at other work.

I am not going to press the point, because I agree with the minister that conscientious objectors come under other departments. But he is an important member of the government, and I would ask him to use what influence he has with the other ministers who are responsible for administering these camps, because it looks to me like a piece of refined persecution to pay men 50 cents a day on this class of work. I agree that there would be a terriffic outcry from the public if you paid them $5 a day, but there is a happy medium. These men could be paid the equivalent of what is paid to men working in the bush, and they should be paid enough at least to pay for their clothing. When talking with some of them I have been told that it takes a lot of overalls and work clothes to do the kind of work they are doing. They should be paid enough so that they will not feel they are being imposed on because of their beliefs. I would ask the minister to consider seriously making some provision for the families oi any of these men who are married, because certainly their families should not suffer because they hold a particular point of view

Items agreed to.
Surveys and engineering branch-Prince Rupert-Terrace-Cedarvale highway, $5,000,000.

Is this $5,000,000 the
expenditure for this year, and what was the expenditure last year on the road, if any? Who are the contractors, and on what basis is the work being done? What kind of contract is it?

The work was undertaken on the recommendation of the Canada-United States joint defence board when there was great urgency to get this work done. A reconnaissance survey was made by engineers
5238	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Mines and Resources
of the surveys and engineering branch of the Department of Mines and Resources. Then firms were asked to tender. As I recall it, there was no public advertisement inviting firms to tender, but all the large contracting firms in Canada were invited to tender, and the basis on which they were invited to tender was unit prices, so much per cubic yard for removing earth, so much per cubic yard for removing rock, and so forth. The work was broken .down into various classifications upon which they would tender. Some eight or ten firms tendered. The work was divided into eight sections of from eleven to eighteen miles each, and competitive tenders were received from at least two contractors for each section.
The surveys and engineering branch had a considerable amount of data in their records as to the costs of road construction in country similar to the Prince Rupert-Terraee country. For instance, several years ago we built the Big Bend highway in British Columbia, and later built a road between Jasper and Banff. So that there was a great deal of information in the department to serve as a guide to what fair costs would be. That information was brought up to date so far as possible by ascertaining the costs of clearing airfields where similar work had to be done.
The tenders were received and the work was started about the middle of June, 1942. It was hoped that it could be completed by the end of last year, but the contractor ran into very considerable difficulty. There was difficulty, for instance, in keeping labour on the work. The wages paid were set by the war labour board, but there was competition for labour, as hon. members know. I think the member for Vancouver East is aware that extensive work was being carried on by the United States authorities in northwestern Canada and that it took some time to get labour difficulties ironed out. For one reason it was difficult, even after -wages were set by the war labour board, to hold men on the work. In addition, there were serious difficulties in carrying on the work in autumn and winter because of rain and snow. Moreover, a section of the road runs very close to the railway. At any rate, for a variety of reasons of which I have given a few, the work did not make the progress which it was anticipated it would make. Last year there was spent on the highway $2,964,000, that is, for the fiscal year to March 31. The vote we are asking for now, it is expected, will complete it.
I should like to emphasize how difficult it is, under all the fortuitous conditions which exist, to make estimates that are accurate. I asked the director of the surveys and engineer-
ing branch, "Do you feel pretty certain that the vote asked for here will complete this work?" He said, "Yes, I think it will, but conditions may arise which will vary it; it might be 10 per cent under or 10 per cent over." But I would hesitate to give even that figure to the committee as a final figure. All I can say is that in the face of very great difficulties the work has progressed and it is expected that some time this autumn the road will be open for, at any rate, fairly light vehicles.
I hope the minister will understand that I am not criticizing at all at the moment; I am trying to get information.
Quite

I realize that there was great urgency for the road in this particular area, after Pearl Harbor. The communications between Prince Rupert and the country to the east might, under the conditions which prevailed, have been closed altogether. However, the minister did not tell me who the successful contractors were in the first instance, and if these same contractors are carrying on at the present time.

I should mention that many of these contractors had to be secured in eastern Canada. Contracts were awarded as follows: section 1, to E. J. Ryan Construction Company Limited, Vancouver; section 2, Rayner Construction, Limited, Leaside, Ontario; section 3, Tomlinson Construction Company Limited, Toronto, Ontario-who have also an office in western Canada; section 4, Standard Paving, Limited, Toronto, Ontario; section 5, MacNamara Construction Company Limited, Leaside, Ontario; section 6, Dufferin Paving Company Limited, Toronto, Ontario; section 7, General Construction Company Limited, Vancouver, B.C.; section 8, E. J. Ryan Construction Company Limited, Vancouver, B.C, Ryans tendered and got two sections.
In regard to the other question asked by my hon. friend: some of the contractors have not been able to complete their contracts. In one or two cases they have given up the contract and it has been taken on for their particular section by one of the other firms, and in one instance, by another firm, the Northern Construction company and W. J. Stewart Limited. I am not certain where their head office is, but I think it is in Vancouver.

Was the Ryan company one of those who gave up the contract and whose contract was taken over by another firm?

War Appropriation-Mines and Resources
Yes, the Ryan company was one of those. I do not know whether it was the only one or not. It had two sections, and arrangements had to be made, I believe, on both.

I understand that after the Ryan company gave up the work, I think for financial reasons, two companies, possibly interlocking companies, known as the Highway Construction Limited and the I. C. Construction Company Limited of Vancouver took over the contract; but I understand that later the contract was sublet to a United States company, the Murphy Company of Washington or Oregon. Has the minister information on that point?
No, we have no knowledge to that effect.
I understand now that approximately $2,900,000 has already been spent-
Up to March 31 last.

-and another five million dollars is asked for to complete the work. A year ago, if I recollect aright, we were told that the whole of the work would cost approximately $5,000,000; so that it is running much more than was anticipated.

This item brings to the committee one of the most important parts of the war appropriation resolution outside of the armed services and matters closely connected with the prosecution of the war. Censorship is a subject which has been engaging the attention not only of the government, but of parliament and the Canadian people. Many things must be done in time of war which will definitely interfere with the peace-time freedoms and liberties of our people, and we take that for granted, having agreed to and voted for participation in war. But the public are as jealous as ever of their rights, their freedoms and liberties with respect to interferences which may come to them in the ordinary course of civilian life, and they take a keen and active interest in censorship. The opening of mail, the tapping of telephones, the inhibitions placed upon the press, and now also upon the radio, as envisaged in the latest directive of the board of censors -these matters demand that on an occasion such as this there should be full disclosure of the policy of the government with respect to interference with the rights of the subject in Canada and its relationship to the war effort.
It has been said many times, but it will bear repetition, that so long as the public is satisfied-and it is the duty of the government to satisfy the public on this point-that these inhibitions and prohibitions and other interferences with personal liberty are in the interests of the war effort, the government can rely upon the public to support to the full the measures which are required. Therefore in bringing to the attention of the government certain features of the censorship, I do so in that smaller field, if I may so term it, wherein there is doubt whether the censorship has gone beyond the point required for security reasons and for the prosecution of the war, and has "slopped over", to use a street term, into a field where the rights of the public are unnecessarily curtailed.
The question of censorship, how far it should go, and alleged abuses of it, have been the subject of newspaper comment in various parts of Canada. I have no desire at this time to cite in extenso the comments made by

War Appropriation-War Services
those who are operating in the field of communications-I mean the press itself. But there has been some uneasiness, and it has given rise to expressions of opinion with respect to censorship of which the government must take cognizance. Recently there have been instances in which the press have taken grave issue on the matter of the extent to which these regulations, directives and orders have gone. Fuel was added to the flame when on June 22 of this year there appeared in one of the national newspapers, the Toronto Globe and Mail, a letter which seems to me unusually significant, because it came, not from a member of the public who is unacquainted with censorship and orders, but from one who has a lengthy and comprehensive knowledge of these matters. I wish to read a letter which was written by Doctor W. J. Edmondston Scott, M.A., who is cited as having been a censor in languages of central and western Europe between 1939 and 1942. This is what Doctor Scott has to say:
The forthright editorial on "Scandalous Censorship" in the issue of June 16 shows that the Globe and Mail still ranks ahead of its contemporaries in being "soond" in doctrine and unusually well informed. From an inside viewpoint it would appear that practically anyone who dares express an opinion on any subject, with or without a political flavour, can have his name put on government files, via the inquisitorial censorship, because of a multitude of topics covered by the regulations, rules and memoranda-from the premier's gossip at funerals down to the abuse of soap and towels. Many folks may say they don't care a hoot; but it's a different matter when some day they discover that, whether in search of jobs through employment or national selective or other government agencies, their chances of obtaining work or preferment, or perhaps the boot, may depend upon what information is listed against their names on file.
"Nation-wide indignation," as you call it, cannot fail to be aroused when Canadians learn the facts-especially employers who stand up against any pressure that may be brought against them to suppress information which is in the public interest to disclose; professional men with a regard for truth but whose freedom of opinion is restricted by inspired attacks in the press on public men and the intelligentsia; as well as the labouring classes, whose union leaders receive the same watchful attention as foreign spies.
And what shall one say of women who are carrying more than their share of the burdens of war? They, too, are taking a deeper interest in the problems of war and peace-a fact that needs no _ comment. Yet this Ottawa racket already visualizes the women of Canada as a potential menace to the principles of democratic government, which the editorial maintains are *being openly travestied by ministers who cling to "the delusion that they are Liberals."
The fact is the Liberal government sees the writing on the wall. It has ceased to trust the people of Canada, so the inquisition is now in full swing. So curious was the cabinet last year in the possibility of women organizing or federating their social and political clubs and IMr. Graydon.j
unions after the war, so as to make their voice heard in the national councils, that a special memorandum, dated May 1, 1942, was issued to examiners which said that:
These are the terms of the censorship regulations:
"All letters observed in the mails containing information regarding women's political activities in all parts of the world and women's activities in connection with post-war reconstruction should be specially submitted to this office and file reference C. 11292-38 quoted."
Reread in the light of the editorial, this should not appear as just another sample of petty politics but a deliberate and frontal attack on the rights and liberties of millions of women *who are being denied the freedom to express their opinions within the law, unless they care to risk the chances of being later penalized, from what the Minister of Justice has styled the "information in his hands."
Worthless gossip, maybe, but immensely potent for backstairs intimidation. Any argument that the cabinet's memorandum ordering the censors to inquire diligently into the private history of women able to express their political views on paper can be correlated to the government's will to victory is refuted by its post-war character.
I bring that to the attention of the house because it has been so widely commented upon in every section of Canada. It is a matter which has evoked interest, and that interest has arisen largely from the fact that this was not just an ordinary person, who knew nothing about censorship, who was writing. Since it has been placed before the public in many parts of Canada, I put it on the record in order that the government may have an opportunity, and the minister in particular, to show the people of Canada exactly where we stand in relation to the matters therein dealt with.
Throughout the country generally there is a disposition among the people to know what is going on behind the doors of censorship in Ottawa. There is a desire, and I believe a proper and well motivated desire, on the part of the public, if they are to have these regulations and these interferences, to be acquainted with the reasons therefor, and in all fairness they should know to what extent the regulations may properly go. It is not too much to ask, and I urge upon the minister that in his statement in reply this afternoon, to the extent that national security will permit, he open the door and acquaint this house and the Canadian people with the exact situation in the matter of censorship, thus clarifying matters and making for much greater confidence among the people.
It is not greatly to be wondered that the average layman is confused about the whole question of censorship. Most people regard censorship as just one of those extraordinary conditions that one must put up with, and

War Appropriation-War Services
they put up with it cheerfully so long as it is necessary for the safety of the state. But when regulations made by ministers of the crown are so interpreted on certain occasions as to indicate that they go very much further, in the minds at least of certain ministers of the crown, one cannot help feeling that the public may properly be excused if they entertain some fears about the extent to which censorship regulations and orders may be invoked. All hon. members, I believe, will recall that in one particular instance in this house, and' it is not so long ago, the Minister of Justice, after an inquiry had been made with regard to the statement of a candidate, a former member of this house, who was seeking office in a provincial contest, expressed his views as reported in Hansard. The candidate in question had made a statement which was allegedly controversial and which allegedly should not have been made against the judiciary of Canada, and a very enlightening reply with regard to censorship came from the Minister of Justice. The hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) had properly asked a question with regard to the incident. Let me read both question and answer so that there will be no dispute on the point. I quote' from Hansard of June 23 of this year at page 3930.
Since no one else has seen fit to do so I should like to direct a question to the Attorney General relating to a dispatch appearing on page 4 of the Toronto Globe and Mail of this morning. A former member of this house, an old parliamentarian and a lady with a keen sense of humour, is alleged to have stated in Kenora last night that "she had never met a progressive judge" and that "judges are all political heelers or they would not be judges." I am aware of the parliamentary rules, hut I want to say that many of these overworked judges have lost their sons in this war, and I think some statement ought to be made in this connection by the Minister of Justice.
Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Minister of Justice): My attention was directed to this short dispatch just a few moments ago. Certainly it is regrettable that declarations of this kind should be made by or attributed to persons so well known as Miss Macphail, who for a number of years was a member of this house. The statement is as unfortunate as it is unfounded. Declarations of this kind can have no other effect than to diminish the respect of the people for the administration of justice in this country, and as such they are most deplorable. I shall direct the attention of the censors to this dispatch, and see if arrangements cannot be made that publicity will not in future be available for matters of this kind.
The answer given by the Minister of Justice opens up in the public mind a whole avenue of questions, because if matters not pertaining to the war, matters which could not by the widest stretch of the imagination have anything to do with national
security, are to be so regarded; if the advisers of the crown are of the opinion that censorship may be extended to that length, then parliament and the country have a right to a declaration by the responsible minister on behalf of the government to show exactly where the public does stand and what the public may expect in the way of further extension of censorship interference. I must confess that in my opinion the matter may well assume serious proportions in this dominion.
I am not going to give any further citations at the moment, but here we have two instances which may perhaps be regarded as examples and illustrations of the sort of thing which may readily occur under a bureaucracy such as the board of censors. I could not wish, nor do I think any hon. member of this house would wish, to take the position that there should not be censorship in time of war. That is something which I think must be approved by this House of Commons. At the same time the question of the care that British people all over the globe have always exercised to see that there shall not be undue interference with the rights of the subject enters into this debate; for in connection with the whole matter of the censoring of news and communications, and all the widespread ramifications over which the board of censors has jurisdiction, we as a people and as a parliament are entitled to know how far the government have gone in unnecessarily interfering with those rights, where the security of the state is not involved. We should know also what is to be the policy of the government in future. What is perhaps more important for us to know is whether the statement made by the Minister of Justice represents government policy. If it does not, I believe the fact of a minister of the crown speaking as he did requires some explanation by the government. If that statement does not represent the policy of the government, then I say the censorship regulations deserve condemnation rather than commendation at the hands of this house. I do not think by any stretch of the imagination this parliament could agree to the proposition that an ordinary statement on a civil matter, which perhaps did not meet the views of the government or certain sections of the people, should come under the censorship regulations.
I leave with the minister those two matters, and suggest that if they are answered satisfactorily it will go a long way toward restoring confidence in the minds of the citizens oj this dominion.

A return was brought down in this house last week with regard to the whole matter of censorship generally. I raised this question When this war broke out. In, the last war the gentleman usher of the black rod, Colonel Chambers, a very able man, was the press censor with only a very small staff. At a meeting with the press he laid down certain rules and regulations which applied throughout the war. In doing, so he followed the British system, which had existed ever since the present Prime Minister, Mr. Churchill, was a war correspondent in the South African war. What was that policy, which I say should have been continued during this war? Here is what I said on November 20, 1040, at page 276 of Hansard:
I believe the time has come wThen the press censorship in Canada should be abolished entirely and we should go back to the good old British system, leaving the responsibility for censorship as largely as possible to the voluntary effort of the press. This is what Britain is doing. There are one or two press censors there who supervise things but the press is left largely alone. In my opinion, it would be far better for the Canadian people, and it would make for the dissemination of more reliable information, if that policy were followed in this country. After all, the press has certain duties to the public. It is the medium through which the government of the day can impart information to the people, and I submit that it should not be trammelled, but should be let tell the truth. Truth is the first victim of this war, and self-respect is the victim of neutrality.
But what happened? A large department was established, and we have seen the result; the public of Canada know less about the war or its causes, or external affairs, than almost any other people in the world. I think the time has come when the whole system should be revised. I fail to see the value of any censorship of publications, or what it has accomplished. Every department of the government issues dozens of booklets. As we all know, members of parliament receive such batches of pictorial papers and booklets filled with pictures that the waste-paper basket has come to be the most useful piece of office furniture we have. Just the other day we received a very beautiful booklet concerning the new $29,000,000 building in Montreal, showing the mural work and all that sort of thing. I hope my hon. friend will not get out a booklet like this about Christie Street hospital-this one on the Montreal station, with its mural work, cards andi pictures and friezes of scenes down through the middle ages. The censors have not interfered with it,

and it is full of gorgeous pictorial decorations from end to end. One picture is just like an opera, or like a musical comedy company giving a performance of Gilbert and Sullivan. Yes, this gorgeous affair, at a cost of $29,000,000, with mural exhibits just to remind us of the Greeks and Romans.
What censorship is there of these American publications? If one goes over to Niagara Falls, or Fort Erie, what does he see? On all the news stands he will find booklets and weekly and monthly publications of all kinds about the mother country and all that kind of thing. If there were proper censorship a lot of them would not be allowed to come in. It was not allowed at the time of the last war, under the old chief censor of those days. And I can tell you this, that as far as this extensive press censorship is concerned I have had to oppose this policy from the start.
I realize there has to be a certain amount of postal censorship. I believe I have sent about half a dozen complaints from people to the minister's department, and he has looked after them very well. But with respect to these publication censors, and their travelling expenses to go round the country, that is quite unnecessary. Only a few days ago news came in from Sicily. That news was censored. The same applies to the north African situation and Canada's part in the desert victory, as I pointed out last spring. Instead of leaving it to the press and the gentlemen of the press- well, if the press did not report other proceedings better than in some cases they report the House of Commons, we might just as well meet in secret. However, I have confidence in the press of the country doing its duty splendidly in this time of war, as they have in the past. Sometimes the House of Commons is itself to blame for not receiving a better report. In these days it is overshadowed by the war.
I appeal to the minister to curtail these affairs, and to consider going back to the old censorship policy. Then, as to pamphlets and booklets, hon. members are getting sick and tired of all these picture books they have been receiving. They would be all right to distribute to the kindergarten or to the elementary schools.

Has there been any change in the policy with respect to the censoring of letters? It has occurred to me there must be some
change in policy, in view of the fact that the services of many of these people were dispensed with not veiy long ago.
I have a question with respect to the censoring of letters addressed to members of parliament, a matter that has been discussed in the house on several occasions. I bring it up again now because not long go I received a letter addressed to me with the letters "M.P." added, and directed to the House of Commons at Ottawa. It had been opened by the censors. If my memory serves me correctly this letter came within the last two weeks, after we had been given some assurance that the procedure was to be remedied. Have any instructions been given to the censors respecting mail addressed to members of parliament? If so, what were those instructions? I would have no objection if the letter had been sent to me at my place of residence, without the letters "M.P.". But I do object strenuously to the censoring of letters addressed to me as a member of parliament at the House of Commons in Ottawa.

take some notes as hon. members have spoken, and I ask nothing better than to speak as openly as public security will allow, with respect to this matter of censorship. So far as I know the censorship we now have, the censorship we are now discussing, is a continuation of the censorship which was instituted at the beginning of the war. But as I have already said, censorship is an essential arm of the services. Censorship exists only because there is a war. We cannot carry on censorship alone; neither can the allied nations carry out their censorship without the every-day assistance of the Canadian censorship. What we want to do is to find out things about the enemy which are of importance to us; his intentions, his activities, so that we can the better safeguard our boys overseas or on the seas or above the seas.' We place a value upon information of this kind perhaps in direct ratio to the degree of desire on our part to know what the German censorship is doing. We feel that if we had all the details of the processes of German or Japanese or Italian censorship we could do a better job and we could ward off dangers to our country and to the people who are fighting our battles.
If you will recall, the motion went to a vote ' the other day and it was defeated. Immediately afterwards the Prime Minister offered to have the matter gone into very carefully and undertook that the Minister of National War Services should bring down such papers as in
his opinion it would be safe to produce to the public. I am still going over some of these papers, although a vast number have been scrutinized already. There are papers which contain no military secrets, but I submit that the mere fact of making them public, as they would foe were they tabled, would tell the enemy things about which he would pay dearly to know if the position were reversed; that is, how he is dealing with this business.
There is nothing we want to hide in this particular matter. I should be very glad to discuss these matters with any hon. member, but I would ask, indeed I would implore, hon. members to remember that we are playing with fire. Are the broadcasts censored which are made by panel speakers over the Canadian broadcasting corporation? Are they censored before being released, or are they released on the responsibility of the person broadcasting?
Mr. LaFLECHE: Speakers may submit their manuscripts to censorship, but they do not have to. If a speaker does not and something goes out which is against the regulations, then the manager of the station is held to account. He becomes responsible.

On two occasions I have directed attention to a charge made by the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen in connection with broadcasting, and I have said the same thing myself, with reference to a broadcast made by Doctor Watson Thomson of Winnipeg some time ago in which he made some startling statements of one kind or another. I also asked Doctor James Thomson in the radio committee whether he had any comments to make and he said he had none. I am wondering if this is the kind of thing that is permitted. Let me read-

I associate myself with the remarks of the hon. member for St. Paul's. The general tone of commentator broadcasting in this country is thoroughly subversive, anti-British and anti-democratic, and it is time some change was brought about and some of these people were taken off the air.

This is a
most inconsistent attitude. This afternoon the leader of the opposition made a very fine speech and the minister made a very fine statement of policy. I hope that what he said is the policy of the government, that censorship should deal only with matters pertaining to the winning of the war and should have nothing to do with interfering with expressions of private opinion in reference to our internal policy or even empire policies. Now, when these hon. members want to use the censorship regulations to take off the air or to restrict in some way Doctor Watson Thomson or anyone else who expresses views with reference to matters that are of concern to all the people of the British commonwealth of nations, then I say you are defeating the very purpose for which these censorship regulations have been set up. I have not only listened to Doctor Watson Thomson's broadcasts; I have been careful to get copies of them, and to check them over. Doctor Watson Thomson himself is a Britisher, not long out of Edinburgh, Scotland, and he has never said anything derogatory to the British empire or subversive to our war effort. He has expressed opinions
which one can hear expressed any day in the week at public meetings in Britain, in the columns of the Times or in Hyde park.

I am not very familiar with this matter, because I have not listened to the broadcasts or read what was said, but is not this the man who took a little time to deal with the Indian situation; and was it not a fact that many people felt that this was a matter which did concern the war effort? Yes, Doctor Watson Thomson did express his opinions with reference to the Indian situation, as have British members of parliament.
Without knowing anything about it.

The fact is that the man has a right to express a point of view contrary to that which other speakers were allowed time on the radio to express, and in my opinion the minister and the government will make a great mistake if they ever tolerate the use of these censorship regulations to muzzle any man merely because the views he expresses do not coincide with their own. I hope the minister will keep to the policy he enunciated this afternoon, under which these regulations will be used to prevent subversive statements or anything that would harm the war effort, but that they will not be used to prevent people from freely expressing their opinions, whether they be in criticism of anyone in this country or even in constructive criticism of other members of the united nations.
