opportunity to make some observations in connection with one of the factors which go to the root of the whole problem of broadcasting as far as public ownership in Csgnada is concerned.
Subject to the provisions of the act, the minister has jurisdiction over the operations of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. As a fairly close student of that corporation for some years, and as a member of the committee which last session went rather deeply into the affairs of the corporation, I think I can state to-day, conscientiously and unequivocally, that one of the real difficulties in connection with the broadcasting corporation lies in the tragic weakness of the board of governors of that institution.
I believe the minister will be the first to agree that if there is one thing the broadcasting corporation needs it is public confidence, which is vital and essential to the success of any agency of communication. As long as the present situation is allowed to continue, however, public confidence cannot be maintained in that institution. You hear this on every side, and I am sure I am reflecting a large measure of public sentiment in this country when I make that statement. This afternoon I make a sweeping condemnation of the board of governors of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. I condemn them on one ground in particular. After the recommendation brought in by the committee last year, I cannot conceive why the board of governors of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation did not resign in a body, for in my opinion, that would have been in the national interest. In expressing that broad condemnation of the board, I am willing to agree that there may be some good men who would have to take part in any such general resignation, but in all fairness to Canada and to the government I believe it was their duty to resign. I have taken that position previously, and I take it again to-day. If there is one thing above another which the broadcasting corporation should seek at all times it is to maintain and preserve a position of nonpartisanship in this country. The people of Canada have a right to demand that there shall not be any shadow of suspicion in regard to partisanship on that board. I am not going to make special mention of the chairman, Mr. Rene Morin, but I will say that I do not think it helped, from the point of view of strict non-partisanship, to appoint as chairman of the board of governors a man who from 1921 to 1926 occupied a seat on the 
government benches in support of the Liberal party. I do not want to condemn him on that ground alone-

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Alone?

Perhaps I should withdraw that; perhaps I was a little more careless in my phraseology than usual. In any event I would say that in itself would not be necessarily a ground for condemnation; but considered together with the situation that exists in connection with another member of that board, it makes a combination which I think should call for a complete reconstruction of the board of governors in the interests both of the broadcasting corporation and of our national life. Some three or four weeks ago the newspapers in this city and other places in Canada carried some interesting news with respect to another appointee to the board of governors. I refer to Mr. E. H. Charleson of Ottawa.
A very fine man.

I expected that would touch a tender spot. If I were in the place of the hon. member for Ottawa West, I would have interjected-but I would have made it more vehement than he has done. I think most hon. members of parliament usually know when they are going to be hit, before they are hit-and that is exactly what happened in this case.
I have never met Mr. Charleson, but I am condemning the system under which a member of the board of governors of an institution supposed to be entirely non-partisan, supposed to cater to the best interests of Canada, one in which public confidence must be maintained at all cost, can be chosen in this way. To say the least, I do not think it was within the bounds of strict propriety, nor do I think it was in the interest of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation itself, or in the interests of Canada generally that a member of the board of governors of that organization should, if the newspaper report is correct-and I have never seen it denied-have been one of those who would preside at the election of officers for the Liberal Association of Ottawa West some three or four weeks ago.
I am the last one who would suggest that there should not be a meeting of the Liberal Association of Ottawa West. That in itself is quite a proper procedure. But I do question -and it is questioned not only by me but by people throughout Canada-the propriety of a man holding a position in an organization supposed to carry the banner of non-partisanship,

War Appropriation-War Services
and at the same time presiding at a political meeting. Yet the government does not condemn this practice in any way. The man in question is left in his position, after having presided at the meeting of the Liberal Association of Ottawa West. To say the least, it was an improper thing to do. And if that is permitted, it would seem there is nothing to hinder any man on the board of governors of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation doing the same thing.
I want to point out what I have pointed out before, namely that we need a new board of governors for the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, a board of governors of which there could not possibly be any criticism. Let us have men and women who are outstanding citizens of Canada. May I repeat a criticism I have made before, namely that of a board of nine only one represents labour. Does anyone seriously contend that one out of nine would be a fair representation of labour's claim in Canada? Of course it would not. Not only that, but we must remember that not one member of the board of governors comes from organized agriculture. On other occasions I have asked the Prime Minister if, when making his appointments, he would make sure that a farmer might be chosen. So far that undertaking has not been given. A farmer has not been chosen, although there is a vacancy on the board.
May I only repeat what I have said on other occasions, that in the interests of this national institution w'e should see to it that the governor takes heed of the public warning I am now giving, namely, that I ask for the resignation of the board of governors of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. Let us have appointed to that board those who can command the confidence of the people of Canada. In any event there should be a wholesale resignation, so that there may be a wholesale reconstruction in the national interest, and also in the interest of the government and of parliament.

I should like to inquire if the capacity to campaign in an election is one of the qualifications for membership on the board. I understand that the member on that board who comes from Nova Scotia actively campaigned on behalf of the Liberal party during the last election in that province. In view of the information submitted to the committee by the hon. member for Peel, it appears to me that to a considerable extent the ability to campaign must be one of the qualifications for these men to serve on the board. It would seem that they would have to be able to campaign at least on a political platform, if not over the air.

I agree with every word said by the leader of the opposition with respect to the report. I do not agree with what is contained in the report. It may be that the recommendations in it were carried out last year by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. But I do not see how the government, in view of that report, can still carry on in the same way, particularly when it was pointed out that the independence of the corporation from partisan control is to be , assured by its constitution.
We had before us in that committee one of the outstanding electrical engineers on the continent, a gentleman who is professor of electrical engineering at the university of Toronto. Mention is made in the report about keeping the channels open. May I point out the importance of filling up our channels, and of taking full advantage of our opportunities under the Havana agreement. I say that already, through the attitude and the policy of the board of governors of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, many of those channels have been lost to Canada. It is all very well to say that under the Havana agreement we may be able to get them back in the future, but all one has to do is to read the observations of Professor Bayly to see what will happen.
The principle followed by radio stations, and backed by governors, is one of "what we have we hold". We must give more power to the private broadcasting stations, and fill up those channels, or we shall lose them, as sure as we are here. This is a technical subject, and one which could not be discussed adequately in the house. However, this question with respect to channels is most serious, so far as Canada is concerned, and I believe we should employ electrical engineers to make a proper survey for us, so that we may know what we are doing. While the subject is technical, yet I would urge upon the government the importance of preserving to Canada the channels we already have, and that we must guard against losing any more. There is no time to be lost. We have until six months before the expiration of the treaty in 1946. It takes at least six months to get the permits and everything arranged and one cannot build a fiftjMbousand-watt station under a year at least, so that there is no time to lose. I commend the reading of the report to hon. members.

May I draw to the attention of the minister a matter which has been drawn to his attention in previous years, but which perhaps may be drawn to his attention this year with a little more force and conviction. Those of us who live in rural constituencies cannot help but be impressed by the changed situation with which our rural mail carriers have to cope. At this stage of the proceedings I do not wish to do more than register a protest with respect to the whole question of rural mail carriers and also to offer a suggestion which may be of some help in dealing with this matter. Faced with low incomes, many of our rural mail carriers have had to live on perhaps as low a level of sustenance as almost any class of people, and in the majority of cases on a much lower level than any who are directly or indirectly connected with the public service. The rural mail carrier, of course, comes very close to our agricultural population. He is part and parcel of the life of the rural people of Canada. I myself can recall in my early days on the farm having no better friend than the rural mail carrier who came to our gate every noon, and I think all of us who are farmers feel the same way about the rural mail carrier who always came regularly no matter what the weather, in good weather and bad. He was a public servant with whom the farmers and rural dwellers seldom found fault. As a class the rural mail carriers in Canada may be said to have carried out their duties in peace time and in war with credit to themselves and to the department with whom they had contracted, and to the satisfaction of the country generally.
But the rural mail carrier is now faced with rising costs of living and with an inadequate additional allowance. I believe it is something like five per cent which he has been allowed to cover the additional cost of gasoline and matters of that kind entering

Supply-Post Office
into his operating costs. Yet he has at the same time seen other branches of the public service-true, technically perhaps they may not be parallel branches; nevertheless they are branches of the public service- receive the cost of living bonus while he is denied that right. I recognize that perhaps from the technical point of view the cost of living bonus would not normally attach to the remuneration received from a contract awarded by tender. Nevertheless I point this out to the minister, and with the sole object of expressing an opinion which is widespread among the rural mail carriers themselves: They feel that they are being treated differently from other branches of the public service, particularly the Post Office Department, in being denied, whatever the technical reason may be, and it may be a good one, the cost of living bonus which is awarded to other branches of the public service. They see the cost of living bonus paid in the one instance and not in the other, and it is difficult for them to understand why this distinction should be made.
I know what the minister's answer will be. But I wish to point out to him that that will not remove the dissatisfaction among the rural mail carriers. I want the minister to make a note of my remarks with respect to one question I asked and that is this: What has been the government's policy with respect to the opening of new tenders or allowing new tenders to be submitted for various routes where the original tenderer has not completed his term of contract but has found himself unable to carry on? I imagine the answer to that question would show a trend which would much more eloquently and adequately show the rural mail carrier situation than any words I could utter in this house.
I am not attempting to leave an impossible situation on the minister's doorstep. No one who has given an intensive study to the question of how to deal with the rural mail carrier situation could fail to recognize that the minister has a problem on his hands. As a private member of this house I have given as much study to it perhaps as most, and I am in a position to say that I have some sympathy with the minister when he attempts to find a solution of the rural mail carrier's troubles. Nevertheless that is not a sufficient reason why there should not be a forthright attempt made to solve these troubles. There have been many more difficult jobs which this parliament has undertaken, and I condemn the government for not at least making an effort to solve the problem once and for all. Surely the fact that the problem is a difficult one should be a challenge to the government to solve it rather than a signal to do nothing
about it. I believe that this session should not have been allowed to reach its present stage without the minister having asked parliament to set up a committee of this house to deal with the problem of the rural mail carrier in Canada. I have sat in this house for some eight years since 1935, and whenever a departmental estimate covering the rural mail carriers has been up for consideration, I have seen men on all sides of the house offering suggestions in this committee of the whole, some constructive, some just suggestions, but all offering criticism, and I have seen the minister, whether it be the present minister or his predecessors, always writhing a little under the criticism but not knowing which way to turn for a solution of the problem.
I make this suggestion to the minister. Perhaps it is too late to set up a committee of the house this session, but if he is unable between now and the time parliament meets again to make any more headway than he and his predecessors have made in the past in solving the difficulties of the rural mail carriers, I think he owes it to the rural mail carriers, and owes it to parliament, and I am not so sure but what he owes it even to himself, to ask for the appointment of a special committee of the House of Commons to find ways and means by which the rural mail carriers may be put in a position at least comparable with other government services, not only in the Post Office Department but other departments as well.
Much good could come out of the calling of witnesses and the taking of evidence of the mail carriers and from the broad discussion which could be had by such a committee. At least it would show the mail carriers that we as a parliament were prepared to come to grips with this problem and, if possible, make recommendations leading to a satisfactory settlement of their difficulties once and for all. We owe them that attempt at least. Their situation I feel is a challenge to parliament and to the government which we have failed too long to take up. I make that suggestion in the hope that it will be accepted by the government to bring about an overdue reform in the situation of the rural mail carriers of this country.

I wish to call to the attention of the minister the fact that the hard times through which we passed in Saskatchewan led a good many of our farmers to tender for mail routes for an absurdly small remuneration. It was a question of getting some income rather than no income. Like the leader of the opposition, I think the Post Office Department must consider the changed
Supply-Post Office

times and the importance of the service being done by these mail route carriers, and the country should see to it that, in spite of particular emergencies which may force some to offer their services for very small compensation, they should receive fair and reasonable remuneration for the work they do.. We expect of them utter honesty and unvarying service in good and bad weather and under all sorts of conditions. I hope the Postmaster General will give most generous consideration to this question of adequate remuneration for rural mail carriers.
One question I should like to direct to the Minister may not come under this item; if it does not, I ask the indulgence of the committee. With regard to the city of Swift Current, as the minister probably well knows, I have been pressing upon the department two necessities. One is the improving of the status of the post office, so that the staff will come under the civil service commission and some provision will be made for those employees who have spent a lifetime in the service of the department. Another is that the city has now reached an importance in size and population which would warrant a carrier house delivery. I would appreciate it if the minister would indicate what attention the department is giving to these oft-repeated requests.

I, too, wish to say a word
about the position of rural mail carriers. It interests me very much because I have been in touch with many of the representatives of the rural mail carriers' association, and in a measure I am in a position to know then-wishes and requests. I can tell the committee from my personal knowledge that the Postmaster General is very much interested in this question and, I am sure, has been trying for many months past to solve the problem. The idea of appointing a special committee of the house to study the requests of these carriers is a good one, if the problem cannot be solved by the department alone. Since the beginning of the war there has been considerable competition in respect of these routes, and it is clear that the tender system, whereby farmers seeking to get some more revenue make bids at too low a price, is not the best system which can be applied if fair and reasonable remuneration is to be granted for the work done. I know of many instances where these men are working at a loss, and it is only fair that carriers should1 receive sufficient payment to make a little revenue out of the work.
I remember the days when I myself was a railway mail clerk and used to meet many of these people. At that time the same problem existed, although it was not then so acute as

it is now on account of the war. I associate myself with all hon. members who would contribute constructive criticism and suggestions to the Post Office Department with a view of rendering justice to these mail carriers. I sincerely sympathize with them, and I know the people whom they serve are well aware that they are inadequately paid. This condition. should be remedied. I repeat that I recognize the anxiety of the minister to find ways and means of settling the problem, and I am sure he is sympathetic to those who are affected by it.

I have one question to ask the minister which I think could be answered before six o'clock. I have a letter from the father of a son who is serving in the Royal Navy, and I will read a part of it. He states:
When w-e send a parcel to our son we are limited to five pounds because he is in the Royal Navy. I sent him one to-day, and it contained one pound fruit cake, one pound assorted biscuits, a small package of dates and a bit of cheese. I figure he would clean that up in an hour. If he had been in the Canadian forces we could have sent him eleven pounds, at least enough to do him overnight. There may be a reason for it but it looks odd.
Is that correct, that we are allowed to send a parcel of only five pounds to those serving in the imperial forces, either on sea or on land, but that we can send an eleven-pound parcel, I assume at the same rate, to those serving in the Canadian forces? If so, it is not fair, because many of our boys have enlisted in the imperial navy, in ships and other services.

I wish to thank the hon. member for Davenport for having brought that matter to the attention of the committee, in order that there may not be any .misunderstanding about it. First of all, as regards the rate, the rate per pound is the same. As regards the weight, the statement he makes is correct, but the regulation about weight is not one made by the Canadian government; it is made by the British government.

I wish to associate myself with the remarks made by the leader of the opposition, the hon. member for Swift Current, and one or two others in regard to the rural mail carriers. This question has been up, when

Supply-Post Office
the post office estimates have been under consideration, for a number of years. If I remember aright, we had this problem during the years from 1930 to 1935, at least before the present Postmaster General took office, and apparently it does not matter which government is in power, it has been found impossible, or at any rate there has been an unwillingness, to do anything. The time has come when we should have more equality in employment, particularly in the public service. We cannot expect private employers tO' attempt any equality in private enterprise unless the government first tries to have equality in the public service. It may be said] and it is said that the rural mail carriers are themselves to some extent responsible for the. conditions under which they work because they outbid one another for these positions. If they do that, obviously it is done because of their necessity and not froim choice. There is no position in the public service, from the Postmaster General down, for which someone could not be found at less money if he had an opportunity to take the position. But that is no reason why there should not be an investigation and some plan worked out by which mail couriers would be given a living wage the same as persons in other employment are entitled to to-day. I hope the Postmaster General will consider what has been said to-day on this question.
There is one other matter to which I wish to refer. I believe it was brought to the attention of the Postmaster General when he visited Vancouver early in the year. The postal employees in Vancouver have some grievances, and although my information comes from that city I understand that this condition is general throughout the postal service in Canada, or at least in the larger cities. I have before me the Vancouver News-Herald, of January 14, 1943, and a report there bears out the statements made to me in correspondence from post office employees in various parts of Canada.
Their first grievance is that order in council P.C. 32/1905, passed on May 10, 1940, set the quota of the permanent staff at, I believe, ninety per cent of the total staff, but that since that time, on account of changes that have taken place in the staff, the ratio of temporary to permanent employees is about twenty to eighty instead of ten to ninety. The way in which this works out is this. Men who came into the service as far back as 1937 are still temporary employees, still on the lower wage of S85 a month. There may be some cost of living bonus or something within the last couple of years. At any rate that is the condition which prevails. Where there is a possibility or, indeed, a probability, as in this case, that these employees will ultimately become a part of the permanent staff they should be taken into the permanent staff after a period of time, regardless of whether they comprise eighty-five or ninety-five per cent of the service as a whole. To fix an arbitrary number of permanents as compared wdth temporaries is, in my opinion, wrong. I am not referring to war workers. After an employee is taken into the normal service and has served a year or a year and a half or even two years as a temporary, he should automatically be taken on to the permanent staff.
Another matter with regard to the Vancouver post office is the large amount of overtime that is being worked, but the only overtime that is paid for in cash is, I believe, about thirty hours during the Christmas rush. All the rest of the overtime is paid for by time off, and as at January 1, 1943, the excess overtime in the Vancouver post office was approximately 18,500 hours. If you have a state of the labour market where there is a scarcity of labour so that instead of having to work less time people are compelled to work overtime, it is utterly impossible to compensate for this overtime by time off. I suggest that the government adopt the policy of paying for all overtime in cash in the same way as it is paid for in ordinary employment.
There is one other grievance which I can state better by reading a paragraph in a letter I received from the national treasurer of Canadian postal employees. I quote:
Our holidays are given on seniority and a junior man (one with less than two years steady employment) may go on his holidays before he has earned his full leave period. After his holidays are over and should he be called to the army, he must refund the money he has received for the days he was on leave that he had not earned. (He is allowed li days per month.) But, and here ig the catch, should he have time coming to him for overtime he has worked, well, he gives that for the good of the post office.
It seems to me that if this matter of time works in one way, in favour of the government, it is only just that if the government owes something to the employee, he should be paid. These things are so small that it is amazing to think the post office authorities would allow them to remain as irritants affecting the morale of the civil service. I hope the Postmaster General will take note of what I have said, and I should be very glad if he could make a statement at this time as to the steps that are being taken to remedy some of these complaints.

I should like to bring to the attention of the minister a matter that has to do with the service given many of our people who live in rural areas; I am not going to say anything in regard to the remuneration of the mail carriers, because the minister has heard enough about that. Two years ago I understood the department was loosening up a little in the regulations governing the laying out of routes, and were granting the privilege of rural mail delivery to people living on what might be described as dead-end roads. We have in my district several such places with which I am personally acquainted, which are not served by the mail carriers, and I wish to draw the minister's attention to the fact that the inconvenience to which these people are put in having to go some distance for their mail is a much more serious matter now than it was a few years ago. They are short of help; perhaps the children have all grown up and left; there may be only the man and his wife remaining on the farm, and they may have to travel some distance for their mail. With the present shortage of gasoline I believe they have a real complaint, for they are taxpayers just the same as the people who live on the other roads, who are given better service. I have in mind one case in particular, of a man who lives on one of our trunk highways, midway between the village in which the post office is located and the cross-road which is travelled by the mail carrier. This man must either go into the village for his mail or have a box at the cross-road, which is a considerable distance away. I should like to ask the minister if in a case like that it would not be possible for the man to get his mail from the bus which delivers the mail to the village.
Last year when these estimates were under discussion I mentioned the closing of a subpost office in the city of Belleville, which meant a considerable hardship to a number of people just outside the city limits and some little distance from the city post office, to which they must go for their mail. This subpost office has been closed now for perhaps a year and a half. I believe it was closed on account of some question over the cost of the building and the remuneration of the postmaster. When we were discussing these matters last year the minister promised to give consideration to this situation, but so far the condition has not been remedied. These are the two items I should like to draw to the attention of the minister.
What is the present remuneration for a full-time postman in the city of Toronto, say, who has been in the service for some years?
And nothing more?
The uniform, carfare, boots, raincoat and the cost of living bonus.
How many holidays with pay does he get?
Eighteen days.
That is about three weeks?
Yes.
I am not going to say anything more about that at the moment, but it does not seem sufficient remuneration for men who have such responsible positions and who perform such arduous duties.

The question of the remuneration of rural mail carriers has been discussed at some length. Recently some confusion has been caused through a war-time bonus which has been granted to underpaid rural mail carriers, at least to help defray some of the increased cost of operation. I believe that matter should be explained at this time, in order to clarify the situation. Many of the mail carriers are under the impression that if the contract is changed by adding a war-time bonus, the contract is broken and will have to be advertised. That is not my understanding, and I should like the matter cleared up. If they are granted a war-time bonus in order to help meet the increased cost of operation, the contract is not broken. After the war, when conditions return to normal, the carrier may decide whether he wishes the contract advertised or whether he wishes to revert to the original terms. If that could be explained at this time, I think it would clarify the situation.

I have a word to say with regard to the rural mail carriers, but before touching upon that matter I should like to pay a tribute to the Postmaster General, who, in my view, in his short regime has fully measured up to the illustrious reputation made by his revered grandfather, Sir William Mulock, in service to Canada.
I believe the department showed wisdom last year, when renewing these rural mail contracts, by increasing in a reasonable and proper way the remuneration paid these mail carriers. In the last five years in my district of Parry Sound I have investigated practically every route and every carrier engaged in this

Supply-Post Office
important work, and I believe every carrier in my district has been and still is underpaid in relation to the service he renders to his country. There is a tradition among mail carriers, and I fancy it is not peculiar to my own district, that his majesty's mail must go through. In the winter time, with six feet of snow on the roads, with a twenty-six mile route, when the car will not start and the roads are blocked, though the horses have to be harnessed to the old sleigh, his majesty's mail must go through. We cannot run riot in the matter of increases; but if my memory serves me correctly, in the last year the department had been more liberal in renewal contracts, in seeing that in deserving cases there have been increases. We sometimes forget the service these men render. I should like to add my voice to those of hon. members who have already said that the rural mail carrier is a splendid servant of the country, and that he should receive fair treatment in his contract.

First of all, the hon. member for Lambton-Kent referred to certain orders in council. I have sent for them, and they will be here in a moment. I shall be glad to give the contents of those orders in council to the committee. .
In the meantime, however, if I may, I shall deal with some of the matters raised by the hon. member for Vancouver East. The hon. member first referred to the question of overtime. May I say to him that I was in Vancouver, and attended a meeting with the officials of the department. We met the representatives of the employees' association out there, and discussed with them their troubles and difficulties. They have troubles; in a large measure what the hon. member has said is correct. And there are troubles of a similar nature at other points across Canada.
I had intended making a statement with respect to overtime, and perhaps this would be the appropriate opportunity. I would point out that the situation in the Post Office Department, owdng to war activities and the depletion of experienced staff by enlistments and the like, has produced a condition with regard to necessary overtime, because most of the work can be handled by men of experience only. It has, therefore, become necessary to meet this condition, on account of the impossibility of liquidating overtime by compensatory time off.
The action taken under the War Measures Act, after a careful review of all post office difficulties, has resulted in the decision that, for the duration of the war, overtime will be liquidated as far as possible by granting corresponding time off. That which cannot be liquidated in this manner by the end of the month following the month in which the overtime was worked, will be paid for in cash at the pro-rata rate of salary which the employee is receiving, provided that the minimum rate of payment shall be sixty cents an hour.
The classes affected throughout the year are postal clerks, senior mail porters, mail porters, postal garage repairmen and postal chauffeurs. During the Christmas heavy mailing period and on statutory holidays the following would be included:	letter carriers, senior letter
carriers, letter carrier overseers, postal garage foremen, and senior postal clerks-the latter only when engaged on manipulative duties.
During normal times, if letter carriers work overtime, the situation is taken care of by a revision of the routes, rather than by payment for overtime.
The second matter raised by the hon. member for Vancouver East was the question of allowing leave at the rate of one and a half days per month of service. This applies to the whole service, I am advised, and is regulated for the service by the civil service commission. I shall draw this matter to the attention of the commission.
Then, the matter in connection with the ten per cent of temporary employees and ninety per cent permanent is one which is receiving serious consideration in the department at the present time. As a matter of fact, it has been brought to the attention of treasury board. I believe I have dealt with the three points raised by the hon. member.
Replying to a question by the hon. member for Davenport the minister said that the annual salary in the Post Office Department was $1,500.
Plus cost of living bonus, plus certain clothing.
In what category would the employee be who received that salary?
I understood the hon. member for Davenport was asking about a man who had been on for some years.

I understood the salary for a letter carrier was higher than that, that he began at $85 a month, and received that amount while a temporary employee. When he is made permanent I understood he received $1,740.

The $1,740 is for postal clerks. The range for letter carriers is $1,020 to $1,500.
Supply-Post Office

As far as the post office service in Toronto is concerned, I should like to sound a note of appreciation of the efficient manner in which the postmaster in that city, Mr. Gibson, has done his work. It will be realized that he has had to work under great difficulties, because the post office at Toronto is at the present time very much overcrowded. Our new post office building is now in the possession of the Department of National Defence, with the result that the post office is operating under a tremendous handicap. Despite that, however, our postal employees are doing a marvellous job. It must be remembered that this is war time, and there is more mail to carry. Our postmen, the fellows on the street, who go from house to house, are always cheerful and always willing to do their best for anyone. If one has any kick about the delivery of his mail, all he needs to do is to inform the postman, and he will look into the matter. I cannot speak too highly of the delivery service we have had under Mr. Gibson, and of the wonderful esprit de corps in the postal service.
There is one improvement I should like to see. It is known that at the present time there are many employees on the part-time list. It seems to me they should be put on the permanent list as quickly as possible, because until that time their position is to some extent insecure. I imagine there are fewer on the temporary list now than there were before, but even so I say that with all the work they have to do in these days they deserve great credit and should be placed on the permanent list.

The Minister of Pensions and National Health seems to want to have this carried in a hurry. Apparently he does not want me to sound the praises of the Post Office Department. I will say that these employees deserve whatever can be done for them; because, after all, I do not think many hon. members would want to shoulder on a hot day one of those big mail bags the postmen carry. As the hon. member for Parry Sound has said, it is his majesty's mail, and the mail must go through.

What has been the success in connection with the carrying of air mail? I understand it was very satisfactory last year. Would the minister indicate the increase in poundage? What is the tonnage, and what is the revenue?

I would advise the hon.
member for Davenport that the number of

pounds carried last year by Trans-Canada Air Lines Limited was 2,308,812; the estimated maximum number of pounds bearing Canadian postage and originating in Canada was 1,771,972; the estimated revenue at $2 per pound was $3,543,944. The estimated profit on operations, allowing a varying amount from fifteen to thirty per cent for write-off for duplications, transfers of mail from one plane to another, United States mail for United States troops, and things of that kind, amounted to $321,573. That was the profit on the operation of Trans-Canada as far as the Post Office Department was concerned. That is quite an improvement over previous years. In 1940 there was a loss of about $1,375,915, and in 1941 this loss had been reduced to $644,762. I am glad to be able to tell the hon. member that the first five months of this year showed a profit of1 $583,514. Last month the number of pounds carried amounted to 315,452, with an estimated profit for the month of $129,005.

Who would be entitled to
these compassionate allowances, and what is the method of disbursement?

Would the Postmaster

The hon. member for
Swift Current has been rather insistent about this matter since I was appointed. We have had a survey made of the situation in Swift Current. At the present time it is serviced from the central office. The survey shows that Swift Current is growing steadily and the growth seems to be of a permanent nature. However, on account of the war we have not been making any new extensions where this can be avoided. It is not only a question of finance; it is a question of conserving manpower. However, the matter is being watched, and if efficient service requires that something should be done, the situation will be reconsidered. I can assure the hon. member that he has not been forgotten.
Are the post office employees covered by any form of workmen's compensation?
The provincial compensation acts are made available to the employees through the medium of the dominion act.

This does not cover
occasional labour?

Is there a complete mailing list available, say in the city of Toronto, which gives the street numbers and so on as revised from time to time? I send out a certain amount of literature as a member of parliament to a great many people in my riding, and I get a certain number of replies. I try to keep my list up to date, but changes are occurring from time to time. I was just wondering if a list were available which people could consult.
No.

It might save a
lot of trouble if the mailing list were made available, because when a person takes a piece of literature out to a man's address and finds he is not there he has to bring it back and then it has to be mailed back to the sender. I could never understand why the mailing list was not made available to the people. We had an example in Montreal lately in connection with an enumeration containing several wrong addresses, which could have been checked if a mailing list had been available. Would the minister tell me why it is not available?
Because it is a householder's list; it is addressed to a house, not to an individual.

Some time
ago I brought to the attention of the minister conditions in the barracks at Saskatoon. In his reply to me at that time the minister said, as reported at page 3160 of Hansard:

before me at the time gave me that information.

361. Canals - Operation and maintenance, $2,529,992.
May I ask, in reference to the Rideau' canal, what it costs to operate, how many employees are engaged in operating the canal, and what tonnage passes through the canal per year?
In 1942, 171 vessels and 1,727 tons of freight passed through the canal. The cost of operation was $188,800.

What tonnage passed
through St. Andrew's locks on the Red river?
I have not that information.
You cannot send a boat down the river from Winnipeg without its going through St. Andrew's locks. They are north of Winnipeg on the Red river in Manitoba.
I do not think it is administered under the canals branch; it must be administered under the harbours board.
If the minister has not the information on hand1, it will do at another time.	.

Has any consideration been given by the department to construction of the Chignecto canal in connection with the defence ministries? It is considered by many who have given attention to the matter of the construction of this canal that if it were in existence at the present time, it would be a valuable military and naval asset; it would reduce the mileage and the dangers of transportation on the Atlantic coast and the St. Lawrence. I should also like to know whether there have been any negotiations with the United States authorities with respect to the construction of this canal, along the same line as the negotiations which were carried on with respect to the Alaska highway. I can understand there may be some necessity for secrecy in these matters. On the other hand, it is not likely that it could be built to serve in the present war, but existing world conditions and naval and military requirements would indicate an urgency for the construction of this canal, purely from a military point of view, leaving all to the good the desirability of having it as a commercial transport route. The minister understands, as do hon. members of the committee, that this canal was projected two or three hundred years ago by the early French settlers, and it would have been constructed many years ago if some engineers who were ultra modern but who, as conditions have developed, were impractical, decided that a ship canal should be constructed there to give transportation to vessels and shipping across the isthmus. The isthmus is about fifteen to sixteen miles distant. Could the minister give a statement with respect to this matter, and has he had any conferences with the ministers of defence or the United States authorities?

Since I have been in the department, no consideration has been given to this project, and I believe that none has

Supply-Transport
been given to it since 1939; that is, since the war started. No demand that I know of has been made on the department for the construction of this canal for military purposes; none has been made by the United States, and no negotiations have been carried on with the United States since the war began. I believe it would be a good post-war project, for consideration as soon as the war is over.
Mr. MaeINNIS: I have received a complaint from employees of the Welland canal, linemen, bridgemen, wiremen, weighmen, and statistical clerks. These men, I understand, are dissatisfied with wages and working conditions, and apparently they have been unable to get satisfaction from the department. They made an application for a board under the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act and asked the department to concur in the recommendation. I have here a letter dated June 28, 1943 and signed by the deputy minister of transport. It is short, and I will read it:
Dear Sir,
I have your undated letter enclosing an application signed by a number of employees of the operating staff of the Welland canal, seeking the appointment of a board of conciliation to consider grievances concerning wages and the methods of promotion now in effect on the Welland canal. Upon inquiry I am advised that the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act, under the provisions of which boards of conciliation and investigation may be established, is applicable to industry only, and not to the public service of Canada.
In view of the fact that apparently these employees cannot go before the tribunals set up by the government to deal with the grievances of persons in the employ of private companies and now, I believe, in some crown companies, what procedure is available in the department to adjust grievances? Is there any machinery by which employees can get their grievances heard? There is considerable information in the file which was given to me, but I have had it so short a time that I have not been able to make myself acquainted with its contents, and consequently I am not in a position to judge definitely as to what they want.

I thank my hon. friend for having given me the information and read the letter. I gather that these employees are permanent members of the staff or in the position of permanent members and they would come under the jurisdiction of the civil service commission, which has sole jurisdiction over the establishment of their classifications and their remuneration as well. Therefore their claims for increases of wages
or changes of classification must be addressed to and adjusted by the civil service commission.
Mr. MaeINNIS: I wonder whether the minister and the officers of his department gave consideration to the fact that war conditions have considerably upset normal relations in the matter of wages and working conditions. I think that particularly applies in the civil service, where conditions are much more rigid than they are in ordinary private service, or in places where employees are more free to organize and put forward their claims. Government employees see on every hand other workers improving their position, either by way of increased wages or cost of living bonus, or considerations of that kind, by making application to the various boards which the government has created to adjust their differences, although these government employees themselves cannot appeal to any such impartial tribunal to settle their disputes. Is there any way by which these people can be heard?

So far as I am aware, there is none apart from appeal to the authority under which they are working. Those classes of employees who come within the jurisdiction of the civil service commission must appeal to the commission for readjustment of their salaries or remuneration. They can always appeal to the head of the department, but even then the head of the department cannot override the decisions of the civil service commission except by act of parliament.
Mr. MaeINNIS: That being so, when they write to the ministers' departments in matters of this kind would it not be a good policy for the head of the department to direct them to those persons to whom they should appeal in order to have adjustments made? There is nothing in this letter except the statement, "I am advised that the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act does not apply in your case," and they are left without any direction. I suggest that the officers of the department should direct them and should take a little more human interest in these employees than merely to give them a negative answer and say, you are in the wrong pew and there is nothing more to be said; you had better get out.
If letters are addressed to the minister the writers will receive such direction as it is possible to give them.

I believe it was the day before yesterday, or yesterday, that I handed to the Secretary of State, with reference to the
Supply-Transport

Welland ship canal operating and administrative staffs, in connection with whom complaints had been made, the correspondence in the matter with the understanding that an investigation would be made. Seeing that the minister whose estimates are now before us is directly involved, I wonder if the Secretary of State has conveyed to him any report that has been made in pursuance of the investigation which he promised to make for me.
Not yet.

May we expect something before the end of the session? I do not want the government to fall into the habit of allowing things to die at the end of the session, because that is a habit which I fancy is easily acquired. I hope it will not be too assiduously cultivated by the administration.
I can assure my hon. friend that the representations in this matter will not die, but that as soon as possible they will be given consideration.

Mr. MaeINNIS: I have some questions to ask with reference to the loss of the ss. Northholm, near Cape Scott, last winter, into which an inquiry was held.

I am under the impression that a return was made on this matter.
Mr. MaeINNIS: I do not know about a return, but the minister was good enough to send me a copy of the court's report, and it is on the strength of that that I wish to ask a question or two. The ss. Northholm foundered some time last winter-I have forgotten the date-with the loss of fifteen men, all of the crew, I believe, with the exception of two who survived, from the number who got away in lifeboats. I ask this question because I believe that someone is to blame for this loss of life in allowing this vessel to go to sea under the conditions that obtained. I have here the questions which the court was requested to answer. I do not know who formulated the questions, but here they are: Question: Did the master of the ss. Northholm take all reasonable means to save (a) the vessel, (b) the lives of those on board?
It is perhaps significant that the vessel comes first and the lives of those on board come second. The answer is:
The court thinks that more determined steps might have been taken to save the vessel and the lives of those on board, but in the absence of further evidence is not prepared to make an adverse finding in this regard.
Question: What was the cause of the loss of the vessel and the loss of life?
Answer:	(a) Insufficient margin of stability
and insecure battening down of hatches.
(b) Lack of leadership in getting the men into the lifeboat and away from the ship.
Question: Was the loss of the ss. Northholm caused or contributed to by the wrongful act or default of Frank McMahon the master, Ray Perry the mate, the owners or charterers, or any of them, and if so, which of them?
Answer:	The charterers' marine superintendent knew of the improper practice of battening down hatches as was done in this case. Subject to this, and to the answers given to questions 4 and 5, no wrongful act or default was shown.
These are the answers to the specific questions asked, but there is an annex to the report. I should like to put on record a part of this report, because I am satisfied that someone failed) to carry out the proper inspection, with the result that fifteen lives were needlessly lost. In the annex to the court's findings it is stated.
The court is of the opinion that with the deck cargo loaded as it was, the ship was not in a fit condition to proceed on the contemplated voyage, and that this was at least a contributing factor to the disaster that followed.
It should be noted that the ship was lost in a sea that was not considered at all rough. It was not a loss at sea on account of a storm; it was, as the court points out, a loss at sea on account of the way in which the

Supply-Transport
cargo was placed on the ship-I do not know the proper term for it-and because the ship was loaded beyond her capacity. The annex continues:
The court is also of opinion, after giving full consideration to all the evidence, to the material filed, and to the theories advanced, that when the vessel left Port Alice she did not have a sufficient margin of stability; that during the passage to Cape Scott such margin disappeared, due to water finding its way through the improper hatch coverings, saturating the deck cargo, and percolating into the hold. This resulted in an increasing list which eventually laid the engine room and stokehold open to the sea, and caused the vessel to founder.
The court, in view of the special features of this inquiry, thought it well to hear certain hearsay evidence which was tendered. In coming to its conclusions such evidence was ignored.
There was great difficulty in getting evidence in the case, because all but two of the crew had been lost, and the evidence of the two members who were saved after a terrible experience at sea, during which three or four others in the same boat had perished from the cold, was rather inconclusive or perhaps incoherent. From what I have read, however, and from the whole of this report I think responsibility should be placed on someone, because someone was guilty of allowing this vessel to go to sea under the conditions outlined in this report. I should like to know what steps the minister is taking to place that responsibility where it belongs.
In the first place the hon. member understands that this was a private boat, not a boat owned by the government.
It was not a boat owned by the government, but has not the government a certain responsibility, under the Canada Shipping Act, for the inspection of boats, of tackle and all that pertains to boats?

I quite agree, but I wanted to establish that point first for the record. Under the Canada Shipping Act there is responsibility for inspection and also for checking the conduct and qualifications of certificated officers, if there were any on board, and there must have been at least one. All these matters have been investigated to a certain point. As to placing final responsibility by the department on any one person, I must confess that we have not yet reached that point. The findings of the investigation which was held, part of the findings of which has been read by the hon. member, have been under consideration; we are in communication with the marine officers on the Pacific coast with a view to clearing up this situation, but we
have not yet come to a conclusion as to who is directly, finally responsible for the accident.

368.	Marine service steamers, including icebreakers-maintenance, operation and repairs, $1,357,000.
Will any part of this money be utilized in keeping open the channel between Tormentine and Borden?

This money is for the operating expenses of these boats. They are on regular runs, and unless they are assigned to a particular duty at a particular time they are not required to take special assignments or runs. It has been done when required, when any of the ice-breakers were available, and could reach the place.
Is the channel between Wood island and Cariboo kept open during any of the winter months?

There was some discussion with respect to the matter of transportation between Prince Edward Island and the mainland earlier in the session. Since that time, has any progress been made with respect to the procurement of a suitable ferry boat or a more adequate stand-by in the event of any serious accident to the present boat? There is no necessity to repeat the urgency for this provision, because the entire traffic from the mainland to Prince Edward Island depends upon this ferry service, which, as everybody recognizes, is inadequate. What progress has been made in the last two or three months with respect to procuring a new boat, or a stand-by for the present boat?

It has been impossible to find a suitable boat on the north American continent. With regard to procuring a standby I would say we have one specifically assigned to be used as a stand-by to the Prince Edward Island in the event of an emergency. But some progress has been made in developing the plans, if it is built in Canada, of a larger ferry boat which would be the main ferry between these two points. Under those circumstances the Prince Edward Island would revert to the position of stand-by.

Marine service-
369.	Construction, maintenance and supervision of aids to navigation, including salaries and allowances to lightkeepers, $1,980,128.

Has any effort been made by the department to improve navigation on the Mackenzie river? At this time of the year, and in any event a little later in the season, north of Great Slave lake there is swift water, and it is necessary to pull the boats up the river. This is done by the use of a capstan and a long cable. Down the river there is considerable traffic, amounting to many thousands of tons a year. These are good boats, and passengers find it bothersome to have the ship anchored in the middle of the river and to have to wait until someone goes up the river with the cable, connects it on the shore to the capstan so as to pull the boat up the river. It is about time something was done by the department to improve navigation on that great river. I believe there is no doubt traffic would increase if the service vere improved.

The only work by way of improvement which has been done in that section in the last few years has been some dredging by the Department of Transport. I understand that the Department of Public Works has done some other work, but I am not familiar with the nature of it.

Item agreed to.
Marine service-
370.	Agencies, salaries and office expenses, $286,165.
What is meant by the term "agencies"?

They are the different marine divisions in Canada ranging between Prince Edward Island and Victoria. They are at Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Quebec, Prescott, Parry Sound, Victoria and Prince Albert.

Item agreed to.
Marine service-
371.	Maintenance and repairs to wharves, $5,000.
Is $5,000 sufficient to maintain and improve wharves?

The major repairs to wharves in Canada are made by the Department of Public Works. This refers to minor repairs to certain wharves from which we derive some revenue. We employ at least the amount of revenue we get from them in making repairs to suit the convenience of those using the wharves.

Where are those
wharves?
There are about 2,000 across Canada.
That works out to about $2.50 each.
About that.

I suggest this item should be cut out altogether, and the money taken out of the ordinary vote for public wharves, which is something like $100,000 for British Columbia alone. This item is a perfect nuisance in this sense: the rule is that any expenditure on a public wharf under $50 is done by the marine branch. If it is over that amount it must be done by the Department of Public Works. This very often results in confusion. Someone will report that a wharf needs repairs. A man will be sent, at an expense of about $100, to look into it. He may decide that the amount required to make the repair is $48.50, and therefore he washes his hands of it and makes a report to the agent of marine. Then, he will send a boat out or perhaps makes an inspection himself, and finds that the expenditure required would be $51.80, and that, therefore, he could not do it. Then it goes back to the Department of Public Works.
The Department of Public Works maintain an efficient staff of competent men, men who are thoroughly familiar with the making and repairing of wharves, and they go round periodically to make inspections. It would save a lot of trouble and bother if this were all under that department. The agent of marine looks at lighthouses, and things like that. It would be much better, and it would save a lot of trouble if wharf repairs were done by the Department of Public Works. Officials of that department make periodical inspection every year or as often as necessary; when they find little repairs are needed, they cannot do them, and they have to be taken over by the other department, with all the red tape and intercommunication involved. I cannot see how anything is a bit better, and certainly the public service is worse off with this arrangement, and we have a good deal of unnecessary trouble.

I am glad of the suggestion made by the hon. member, and we will take it into serious consideration. Wharves are looked after by the Department of Transport, although they are built by the Department of Public Works. Lightkeepers are authorized to make minor repairs. They may repair a light when they find it is damaged. In the different buildings there are stoves and heaters which sometimes require minor repairs, and they are authorized to do

Supply-Transport
them up to $50. It may be better to have this done under Department of Public Works, and I shall look into the matter and make a recommendation.
I was not talking about the lights, I was talking about public wharves.

It seems to me that one might as well move that the vote be reduced to one dollar because I think it is silly to have it in here. However, I shall not do that now, but do not let us have it in the estimates next year.

Item agreed to.
Marine service-
STS. Administration of pilotage, $142,510.
Does this cover the great lakes or just ocean ports?
Wherever there are pilots.

Item agreed to.
Marine service
STli. Life saving service, including rewards for saving life, $43,560.

Session after session, as this item has come up, the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) has taken a very active part in the debate, referring particularly to the need for life saving facilities on lake Simcoe, the lakes of the Muskoka district and the general lake Ontario area. The hon. member has suggested some important reforms in connection with life saving, pointing out, as the minister will recall or certainly as his predecessor will recall, that many sections of the lake must rely for life saving facilities upon what is supplied by metropoltan centres like Toronto. I draw this to the minister's attention and ask him if any such reforms have been made by the government. May I also inquire who have received these rewards during the past year ? I think it would be a matter of national pride and interest to have on the record the names of those who have been rewarded.

The government has not yet decided to establish life saving stations on the inland waters of Canada. The only stations we have are on the Atlantic and Pacific coasts. We have not the names of those who have received rewards during the past year, because these are made by the humane societies, not by the department. A list could be procured and given to my hon. friend.
I think the minister could consider adopting this suggestion. It often happens that those persons who are rewarded do not receive the recognition in the house to which they are entitled.
I think the suggestion is a good one and I will see that it is carried out.

The particulars of this vote to be found on page 219 of the estimates show four coxswains, four engineers and one second coxswain, or a total of nine men. There cannot be much life saving done with such a small number of men. The city of Toronto has its own life saving crews and equipment. I do not know whether Hamilton has, but I presume it would have similar crews and equipment. To what cities does this vote apply?
It does not apply to any city.

Where are these nine
people operating from?
My information is that there is a most efficient life saving station at Toronto operated by the city.
I said that.
The stations operated by the department are at Banfield, British Columbia; Clayoquot, British Columbia; Bay view, Nova Scotia; and Littlewood island, New Brunswick.

Toronto and other ports on the great lakes have most efficient life saving facilities. A greater tonnage of ships passes through the Soo canal than through any other canal in the world. In spite of the great number of ships that come down through lake Superior to lake Huron and lake Ontario, we do not get a nickel from the dominion government for life saving services. Toronto and other places on the Georgian bay have life saving crews, and I am proud of the work that has been done. Over a- period of years loss of life on the great lakes has been quite small when one considers the difficulties of navigation and the lateness in the year, some time toward the end of December, that grain is brought down. It is only on two or three occasions that there has been any loss of life.

This amount has been reduced by over $1,000,000, with which reduction I am sure everyone is pleased. I have noticed lately that the water in Montreal harbour is higher than in other years, and I would ask the minister whether one of the reasons is the diversion into the great lakes of water from northern Ontario, particularly from the ICenogami river.
I am told that the increased volume of water in Montreal harbour this summer is on account of natural conditions, not to any diversion of water.

Whoever gave the minister that information has not given him correct information. Item agreed to.
Railway service-
Repairs and expenses in connection with the operation and maintenance of official railway cars under the jurisdiction of the department, $39,370.

In the Fraser
Valley to-day we have to transport haymakers from one district to another and we are not permitted any extra gasoline for that purpose. This is in order, Mr. Chairman,

and I want it to be put on the record. It has to do with the railways. I quote from the Ottawa Citizen of to-day's date:
On Tuesday night another special will be sent up to Connaught park. Some of the horses will be vanned up and by Thursday next there will be about four hundred thoroughbreds within the Connaught park enclosure.
In British Columbia a van means a truck, and I feel bitterly that we are not allowed extra gasoline to transport haymakers from one part of the Fraser Valley to another while race horses for Connaught Park can be put into vans and hauled up and down the country.
Order. The discussion must be relevant to the item before the committee, which has to do with official railway cars.

All right. I do not particularly care that some people from British Columbia seem to agree that I am out of order on this point, but I feel bitterly that railway cars should be used to transport horses for race track purposes, so that officials of the wartime prices and trade board can play around at Connaught park when the farmers of my constituency cannot get extra gasoline to transport haymakers to where they are needed in the Fraser Valley.
Order.
If I am out of order, Mr. Chairman, I will sit down.
The hon. member is out of order.
The hon. member for Fraser Valley had the floor, and if he is out of order I think the Chair should state why he is out of order.
Order.
I brought to the attention of the hon. member that the discussion must be relevant to the item before us, which has to do with official railway cars and not race horses.

I may possibly be out of
order too, but the first items were passed so quickly that I was not quite prepared. In certain small stations a certain amount of business has to originate before the railways will maintain an agent there. There is a rumour that the railway companies are asking the board of transport commissioners to have that amount of business increased. I would ask the minister if there is any truth in that rumour, and, if so, will the people in the

Supply-Transport
district have an opportunity of making an appeal to the board of transport commissioners?

I think the hon. member is right in saying that it is the policy of the railways to require a certain amount of business at a station to maintain an agent there, but I could not say whether the railways have made application to the board of transport commissioners to increase the amount of business required to maintain an agent. The department has not yet been informed of that.

In case such an application is
made by the railways, would the minister see that the districts affected have an opportunity to present their views?
Certainly.

I have one more question in
connection with, a decision made by the board of transport commissioners in March, 1942. It is in connection with decisions which have been made by the board of transport commissioners in March, 1942, and again recently, opening up the facilities at railway stations, even where elevators are located, allowing truckers to use their mechanical loaders which they have on their trucks, as well as portable loaders.
I have no knowledge of such an order.

I just wish to make a protest
in connection with this. Farmers and farm organizations have been working hard in order to get the grain act amended so that abuses of the grain trade may be done away with; but if this decision stands and this practice is permitted to continue, I am afraid that a number of old abuses which took years to get rid of will be brought into being again. I am making this plea because I understand that certain companies are sending their agents out to the farm, buying bins of grain on sample, and at a certain price per bushel; . there is no guarantee of grade, dockage or weight. They hire these trucks with mechanical loaders or in some cases use portable loaders at sidings to load the grain, and in some cases it has been found that the car leaks before it gets to the terminal so that the farmer loses the amount of grain which leaks out along the way. Several other abuses have been indicated to me. I would ask that this decision of the board of transport commissioners be gone into again with a view to withdrawing from truckers or truck companies the right to use their mechanical loaders or portable loaders at places where elevators are available. I am quite satisfied that a farmer or a number of
72537-333}
farmers shall use their own mechanical loaders and portable loaders for their own accommodation; that is a right principle; then the farmers are looking after their own interests.

Item agreed to.
Railway service-
383. Hudson Bay railway-Construction and improvements-capital, $61,000.

The Hudson Bay railway has served a useful purpose and in the future will prove much more serviceable. A great many changes are taking place in these days in connection with railway transportation and haulage, particularly in respect of motive power. Would the minister give a little statement as to what is taking place in the development of motive power for the Hudson Bay railway? At the present time it is most important that we should have on all the main railway systems every locomotive which can possibly be handled, but at the same time the Hudson Bay railway needs to be serviced. Developments which have taken place include diesel electric locomotives, turbine locomotives, and things of that kind. What is being done by way of providing the necessary motive power as well as releasing such power as can be made available for other railways?

The Hudson Bay railway proper does not own any equipment. All the equipment used on that line is rented from the Canadian National railway system. I do not know of any plans whereby special equipment is being designed or manufactured for that railway. The only equipment which is being used is of the kind required for the moving of freight and of passengers occasionally.

I suggest that we might discuss items 383 and 384 together. I think they are both on the same basis. The minister's remarks do not answer my question. As Minister of Transport he ought to know something about the Canadian National Railways as well. He says that all the equipment is being hired from the Canadian National Railways. I should like to know something about the whole situation. How much freight is going over the Hudson Bay railway at the present time; what are its requirements, and why is $200,000 needed in the current year? I suppose it is to take care of debts. What equipment have we there, and can it be replaced if necessary with other equipment?

I just informed the hon. gentleman that we have no equipment on that road. What is being used is the equipment of the Canadian National railways, which operates
Supply-Transport

that Churchill branch. The government built the line, but it is being operated by the Canadian National railways, whose equipment is being used, as on any other section of the Canadian National railway system.

That does not
answer the question. I have had so much respect for the minister based upon his administration of the Department of Fisheries [DOT]that I thought that probably, when he got to this new position, he would be able to tell us all about it, for he is quite versatile. What I wish to know is the position with regard to the Canadian National and the Hudson Bay railways. Does the government operate the Hudson Bay railway, or is it leased to the Canadian National railways? What equipment is used, and is a deficit unavoidable? Are we using the road to the best advantage?

I have already stated
twice that the Canadian government does not operate the so-called Hudson Bay railway. The railway is being operated by the Canadian National railways on behalf of the Canadian government, and all the equipment used belongs to the Canadian National railways. There are two regular trains each week which operate from July 11 between the Pas and Churchill. 'One is a mixed train with sleeping and dining-ear accommodation, and the other is a way-freight with day coach only. No grain was moved for export during the year, the elevator at Churchill remaining filled to capacity with grain handled in previous years.
Why do we put up $200,000 and $61,000?
That is for the coming year. I mentioned 1942-43.
Why do we need this money?
It is to cover any possible deficit for the current year.
I have one suggestion to make. Would it not be better if the Canadian National Railways took over the railway and ran it?
That is what they are doing; they are running it.
Then, why do we need to have $200,000 in the votes? Why does it not come out of the Canadian National Railways?
I thought my hon. friend knew the history of the Hudson Bay railway.

Yes, I understand
it.
If the hon. member understands it, why such questions?
Why not let the Canadian National Railways take it over and run it?
Is the $61,000 not for capital expenditures, included in which are new sidings?
Yes.

Which are very necessary. I congratulate the people who are operating the railway upon reducing the deficit from $490,000, as shown in item 384, to $290,000. It shows what can be done by the management. It is a good management. I know some of the men at the Pas, and they deserve credit for what they have been doing.
