Items agreed to.
Maritime Freight Rates Act-
385. To hereby authorize and provide for the payunent from time to time during the fiscal year 1943-44 to the Canadian National Railway Company of the difference (estimated by the Canadian National Railway Company and certified by the auditors of the said company to the Minister of Transport as and when required by the said minister) occuring on account of the application of the Maritime Freight Rates Act, between the tariff tolls and the normal tolls (upon the same basis as set out in section 9 of the said act with respect to companies therein referred to) on all traffic moved during the calendar year 1943 under the tariffs approved on the eastern lines (as referred to in section 2 of the said act) of the Canadian National Railways, $3,350,000.

The Minister of Transport was formerly Minister of Fisheries, and many times he and I had arguments across the floor as to why we in the central provinces cannot get fish at reasonable prices. I am going to bring up this question again.
Because you do not go fishing.

I am quite serious; all joking aside. In these days when there is such a scarcity of meat we wonder why we in the central provinces cannot have the railways carry our fish to central Canada so that the people in Toronto, instead of having to pay at the present time 20 cents a pound for codfish, might get that fish at a more reasonable price. I am discussing this matter because the minister has occupied both positions. We have to pay 20 cents a pound and the fisherman in the east gets 2 cents a pound; it used to be three-quarters of a cent a pound.

Supply-Transport
In certain seasons of the year the people in the maritime provinces have shad, and ale-wives, which are a delicious fish if you do not mind taking out the bones. The minister knows all about this and he can tell us why we cannot get their fish. We in Ontario, the people on lake Ontario, are doing a very good job. I see the minister representing the Hamilton district coming in. He knows what a good job his people are doing, selling whitefish and getting marvellous prices for it. It helps in our balance of trade. Why can we not get some fish from the maritime provinces? I do not see how anyone can possibly account for the difference between 2 cents paid to the fishermen there and 20 cents charged to the consumer in Ontario. It is a shame that these fish are used as manure. I repeat, I cannot understand why we cannot obtain shad and gaspereaux from the maritime provinces. Cannot the minister do something about getting fish from the maritimes to us in Ontario? The people in the maritime provinces have always complained that we can ship our products there, while they have no opportunity to reciprocate. I am pleading with the minister to give them an opportunity to send their fish to us, because this comes right under the head of railways. That is where it belongs- transportation, refrigeration and so on. Perhaps in that part of the country they do not get ice; the hon. member for Queens-Lunen-burg (Mr. Kinley) will tell me. At any rate we could not ship our ice from Ontario to freeze the fish there. Surely something could be done about the matter. I have brought it up four or five times, and I am trying to do it to-night in a humorous way. We have spent thousands of dollars to get the people fish-wise -not fishwives.
Alewives.

This is the first time I have been able to corner the minister now that he has had experience in both departments, and I urge upon him that he do something to make it possible for us to get products from the maritime provinces. We will take their fish, but I do not see why we should have to pay through the nose for them when some of them are thrown away and used for manure. It is a crying shame that something more is not done to move fish from the maritimes to the people of Ontario. That is all I have to say.

I am glad the hon. member for St. Paul's has a word to say about the fisheries in the maritime provinces. On behalf of the maritime provinces I express appreciation of this vote, which has appeared
in our estimates from year to year. The man who has been responsible to the greatest extent for this vote on maritime freight rates was the late Colonel Gordon S. Harrington, who, I regret to say, passed away two or three weeks ago. He was the person who largely prepared the case and had this recognition given the producers of the maritime provinces so as to compensate at least partly for the discrimination against the maritimes in the handling of freight between that part of the country and central Canada.
I also wish to express again our appreciation of the work of the commission which sat at that time, consisting of Sir Andrew Rae Duncan, from England, the hon. member for Queens (Mr. Macmillan) and the late Judge Wallace. They brought in this finding, which was adopted by the Canadian parliament and which has been of great benefit to the people of the maritimes. Of course no payments to equalize freight rates could ever compensate producers in the maritime provinces for the handicaps under which they operate in relation to the rest of Canada.
The next item has to do with branch lines in the maritime provinces, two of which are in my constituency of Cumberland. It was unfortunate for the residents of that part of the maritimes served by these branch lines that they were not made part of the Canadian National Railways when so many of the other branch lines were taken over. As it is, the residents and producers along these branch lines have to pay a double freight rate. If these lines had been taken over, as was the case with most of the other branch lines in the maritime provinces, the freight rates would be established on a mileage basis instead of on the basis of these small railway units.
I simply wanted to give recognition to those men who accomplished so much for the maritime provinces, and to express the appreciation of the maritimes to the government for continuing this vote.

Item agreed to.
Government employees' compensation-
587. Administration of the Government Employees' Compensation Act, $24,735.

Is this the item, together with the statutory item just below, under which the rather extraordinary expenditures in the Montreal district which were aired in the house a short time ago, in connection with Doctor Chartier, would come?

Part of it would come
under this item and part under the war vote.
Supply-Transport
In view of the revelations made in the house at that time, has the minister conducted any investigation in regard to that matter? If so, I should like to have his report.

I have made an investigation, and I find that there was no revelation except the amount of money that was paid to Doctor Chartier for his professional services, which was disclosed at the request of the hon. member. The dominion compensation act provides that federal employees in the provinces shall be compensated for injuries or accidents under the provisions of the provincial laws. The compensation act of Quebec provides that dominion employees come under schedule 2, and the government is directly responsible for compensation to the employees for injuries, medical services and hospital fees.

I think the minister gave this explanation on the previous occasion. I was not asking for a repetition of that explanation; what I was really seeking was some report by the minister as to whether or not, after investigating the rather large fees which had been collected from the government by Doctor Chartier, the government had come to the conclusion that the amount was extraordinarily high and, if so, what the government intended to do about it.

The inquiry I made satisfied me that though the total amount was large, the fees were paid in accordance with the provisions of the workmen's compensation act of the province of Quebec, and were checked in each instance by the treasury department of the federal government. The amount appeared large because Doctor Chartier operates a clinic in Montreal, and his services were resorted to both by the dominion government compensation officers and the provincial commission in following up cases, in regard to both radiotherapy and X-ray work. Many cases also arose in war industries in the Montreal area during the last two years, and many serious accidents which were followed up by the officers of the department required the professional advice of Doctor Chartier and the members of his clinic, whose charges were in accordance with the schedule of fees provided by the Quebec act. We could not reduce those charges, nor could we dispute them; they had to be paid, and I am told that the officers of the treasury department and of this branch "of the service, who have been administering the branch for ten or fifteen years, are satisfied that all the money which was paid to Doctor Chartier and other

doctors was in accordance with the schedule of fees, and that it had to be paid in accordance with the provisions of the Quebec act.

I have no desire to continue the controversy at this time; rather I am desirous of seeing the item passed. I take issue with the minister, however, in regard to the amount which was paid; for despite the casual inquiry which he appears to have made, I must confess that I remain unconvinced that this practice should be continued in the years to come, because I think it is an extraordinarily large amount of money to pay in these circumstances.

discharge of commitments entered into prior to March 31, 1943, and has to do with level
crossings; is that correct?

Item agreed to.
Air service
393.	Air service administration, $11,250.

Over what part of the
air service does the minister have jurisdiction?

The civil aviation, or air service, is administered by the Department of Transport. By virtue of an order in council in 1940 the Minister of Munitions and Supply has kept supervision over the air service, although it is administered by my department. It is jointly administered, but the responsibility, through the order in council, is on the Department of Munitions and Supply for the time being.

This was done in ,1940 when the adminstration of the Department of Transport and the Department of Public Works was placed under the same minister. The Minister of Munitions and Supply, who had initiated the trans-Canada air service, by arrangement with the then minister kept supervision over that branch of the service. Since I have taken charge of the department I have been satisfied with that arrangement, and the Minister of Munitions and Supply and myself have cooperated in administering the service.

I have a word to say about this service. I suppose Toronto was the first place in Canada which showed any interest in air service. We had McCurdy, and many other people who knew a great deal about flying in the early days. Then, a lot of our lads were in the first war-and I would refer particularly to Bishop and Barker. Then we come to an experimental stage, during which Casey Baldwin and John McCurdy were active.
Now, through their effort, and through the efforts of people in the United States, such as the Curtiss boys, we have a marvellous airforce. We have marvellous machines. To-day we hear a lot about the Mosquito, which is being built in Toronto. In that city we are air-minded, and we were air-minded as far back as 1935. We made up our minds we needed an airport. We got busy and made many applications for the installation of that airport. Finally it was installed on Toronto island* That was the logical place for it, so far as civil aviation out of Toronto was concerned. A general election came along, and it appeared that some people were annoyed with that election. The result was that plans for a tunnel between the western gap and the airport were never completed. The reason given was that the airport would not be any good. A project worth hundreds of thousands of dollars was abandoned'-and abandoned for political purposes. The result is that we have not got that tunnel, and must use the ferry boat to cross to the island. I charge this government with non-completion of the tunnel. The airport at Toronto island affords first-class landing facilities both for land planes and seaplanes. Toronto was willing to install the necessary sand pumps required to pump the sand. I am
making these statements only to show what can happen. Now, to-day, if you want to take an airplane, what have you to do?
Get on the plane.
Oh, that is what the hon. member thinks you have to do. He is always on a plane, as far as I can see.
I may be on a plane, but you are in the air.
You are in the sky; but probably a little bit later you will be down lower; I cannot tell now. After years of effort our airport was installed, and it is one of the finest in Canada.
At Trenton, did the hon. member say?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Order; let us get on with the business of the committee.

The hon. member is trying to tell me something, and I do not know what he is saying. I think he said something about Trenton, which is a little village near the Trent canal. Yes; that is the place where the Trent canal goes through- and some government or another spent millions of dollars on it.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I rise to a point of order. There are serious-minded members in this committee who wish to get down to the business before it. I ask you, Mr. Chairman, to keep hon. members to a discussion of the item.
If the hon .member will leave me alone I will go on with what I have to say. I am talking about civil aviation, and I do not see why the hon. member for Vancouver Centre should get so sore about it.
The item under consideration is air service administration. I think what the hon. member is discussing is the next item which covers civil aviation.

I suggest that we take the two items together so that we can make a little progress. We have a lot of difficulty, but we put in an airport at Malton and it is one of the finest in Canada. But there is another wonderful site that could be developed. We must not forget that Canada will be the centre of the air world. Along with the United States, the British empire will be the most important factor in civil aviation,
Supply-Transport

and Canada will be the centre of this air traffic. Toronto, and Winnipeg as well, are going to have no small place in that aviation world. All you have to do is look at the globe and see how close places are when you go over the north pole.
Some mistakes have been made, and one great mistake was made at Toronto. We have one of the finest locations in the world for an airport, but for political reasons an airport was built at Malton. Had this other site been developed a man could go from the Royal York hotel through the tunnel, and take the plane for Montreal or any other place on this continent. Instead of that he has to motor out to Malton over bum roads, or he used to until my leader got after them. I am simply pointing out the mistakes that have been made. We should not overlook Canada's place in the aviation world of the future. At one time the best aviation service you could get was given by the Dutch, and the next best was by the English, but we in Canada will be in a position to give service par excellence, working in conjunction with the rest of the empire.

Item agreed to.
Civil aviation division-

I think this item and the three following items could well be lumped together. J,06. Amount required to provide for the payment during the fiscal year 1943-44 to the Canadian National Railway Company (hereinafter called the national company) upon applications approved by the Min-ister of Transport, made from time to time by the national company to the Minister of Finance and to be applied by the national company in payment of the deficit (certified by the auditors of the national company) in the operation of the Prince Edward Island car ferry and terminals arising in the calendar year 1943, $475,000.

It is not my intention to repeat anything I have said earlier in this session on this subject of transportation to Prince Edward Island; but I believe the time is opportune, on behalf of that province, to plan properly a system of transportation in order to carry out the intent of our agreement with the island when it entered confederation. One clause of the agreement with Prince Edward Island called for a proper system of transportation connecting that province with the mainland. Anyone who travels to that island knows that there is not an up-to-date system of transportation to it. The loss of the ferryboat the Charlottetown, was perhaps a

Supply-Transport
blessing in disguise, though inconvenient at present, in that it gives the government an opportunity to provide a more efficient boat. I have heard rumours, and the transport minister said something about a new boat being built, but has anyone heard anything as to the description of the proposed new boat? I hope it will be constructed with speedy loading and unloading facilities like the ferryboats that connect St. Ignace across the strait with Mackinaw, on the south side. These carry an enormous amount of traffic quite speedily, loading and unloading it. I do not think the ferry that was sunk, the Charlottetown, was as satisfactory as it might have been. I was on it several times and, as far as I am concerned, it could have been more satisfactory from the point of view of loading and unloading automobile traffic. I damaged my car on two occasions, because, as everyone knows, it was difficult going round the decks, the passage being so very narrow, and when you got to the end of the boat you were obliged to back around in order to obtain space to park your car. I hope that the new boat which is being built will provide for rapid loading and unloading of motor cars. I make these observations because, in my opinion, there is no part of Canada more beautiful than Prince Edward Island, no other part that tourists would prefer to motor over. There are just as beautiful parts in every province; every part of the dominion has its own peculiar attractions. But in my judgment this is one province that has not had fair play in the matter of transportation service. Not only should there be proper provision as far as the boat is concerned, but there should be a proper wharf on each side of the strait. I cannot for a moment agree with any statement that the approach is satisfactory on either side of the channel for speedy traffic. I can see how they could be greatly improved, and I am convinced that this is what Canada owes to Prince Edward Island if we are to carry out the undertaking given that province when it came into confederation. I will not give details-this was done earlier in the year-with regard to the amount of traffic moving back and forth. Suffice it to say that the time lost to shippers from the island, and the injustice done to growers there in transportation, warrant our making it possible for the people of Prince Edward Island to obtain more speedy transportation to connect them with the mainland. The mainland is their market. I would ask the minister to interest himself, if it is in his department, in the construction of the boat
that is being built, keeping before him particularly the importance of rapid loading and unloading, proper space on the boat for the parking of motor cars, so that it can be done expeditiously, and proper wharfage accommodation on each side of the channel. I repeat, the time has come when we should carry out the undertaking given to Prince Edward Island for a proper system of transportation.

I must again assure my hon. friend that every attention has been given the problem which he has so much at heart. The loss of the Charlottetown was accidental during the war, and everything has been done in an effort to find another boat to replace her. It has not been possible, and now we have decided to build one. Those whom we consider the best marine architects in the country have been retained. They have already toured North America to see what has been done in other parts in the construction of automobile ferryboats, combining a railway car ferry with an automobile boat. That is a difficult feat to accomplish, operating the boat in tidal waters, loading and unloading it. Instructions have been given the architects to go ahead, and they have already begun to design the most modern ferryboat that they can for the service between the mainland and the island. That is the best we can do under the circumstances, and I hope our instructions and expectations will be carried out.

That is the boat; what
about the wharves?

May I draw the minister's attention to the shortage that may arise of flax for the manufacture of nets. My information is that Great Britain controls the supply of flax, and that Canada has sold her supplies to Britain as far ahead as 1945. The manufacturers are warning the industry that we are likely to be short of flax for nets for the spring of 1944. I do not know where they are made in the east, but in British Columbia they were made by the manufacturers and also by hand by the Japanese, though I am informed that nets made by the Japanese were not as good as those made by the manufacturers. Prior to the war we obtained our supplies of flax from Belgium and France, but those supplies have almost run out. I consider it my duty to bring this matter to the attention of the minister and ask him if the Department of Fisheries is aware of what might occur, and what steps are being taken to see to it that Great Britain releases enough of this type of flax for the making of nets for the spring fishing of 1944. Nets last only from one to three years, and the inferior grades do not last more than one year.
We have been aware of this expected shortage, and have made a request to the Briitsh government, as a result of which we expect to have the necessary flax.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. W. GIBSON (Minister of National Revenue):
speechtext: There is really no mystery about the war-time alcoholic beverages order. It was made on the 16th of December and went back to the 31st of October, 1942. It provided for a ten per cent reduction throughout the country as compared with the quantity of beer produced in the year ended October 31, 1942. Every province is treated on exactly the same basis. There is a ten per cent reduction from the amount released to each province in the previous year. In some provinces the sales had been heavy between October 31 and December 16, and that caused a shortage for the rest of the year in those provinces. In some provinces that shortage was more accentuated than in others.
The reduction was on the sales?
The reduction is on the amount of beer sold by the brewers in each province during that period.

It has come to my attention that in some instances Canadian companies that have received orders from the dominion government to supply and ship overseas goods that were manufactured in the United States have paid duty on these goods when they enter Canada. Goods and merchandise that are manufactured in the United States and are purchased by a Canadian company to be shipped to some other part of the world are not subject to duty when passing through Canada to a port of embarkation. Just why these Canadian companies should have paid duty on these goods manufactured in the United States for shipment overseas is a matter that I would ask to have explained. The duties that have been paid in this way have, I am informed, amounted to thousands of dollars. I am not in a position to state how much has been paid, but I believe that at one port in seven months one company paid duties amounting to about $25,000.
The duty imposed by the government of Canada on goods entering Canada varies in amount, as, of course, the minister knows. In the case of mechanical equipment entering this country from the United States, and that is the kind of goods on which this tax has been paid in some instances at least, the duty is about thirty per cent, to which has to be added the war exchange tax of ten per cent 
and sales tax of eight per cent on the duty paid value of the goods, which makes the tax somewhere about fifty per cent. If duty and taxes are paid on goods of this kind, the cost of the article is increased by at least fifty per cent.
When goods enter this country from the United States a document known as a manifest, which is a notification from the customs officer at the port of entry into Canada to the customs officer at the port of destination in Canada that the goods are on their way, is sent to the customer at the port of destination; and when the goods arrive there, the Canadian company from whom the government is purchasing these goods for shipment overseas, in some instances at least, has gone to the customs house and passed an entry, as it is called; that is to say, paid the duty and taxes on the goods.
The purchaser of the goods is the government-the Department of Munitions and Supply or some other department. The goods come from the United States; they are being sent to Great Britain or some other port of the world outside Canada, and there should be no duty paid on them in Canada because they are only passing through this country. The only reason, it has been suggested to me, why these companies that are selling the goods to the government insist on paying duties and taxes is that their sales are being made on a cost-plus basis, and the payment of these duties and taxes would in consequence increase the amount they would receive from the government.
To give an illustration of the manner in which a transaction of this kind is carried out, a Canadian company-say the General Electric Company of Canada, or the Railway and Power Engineering Corporation-receives an order from the dominion government to supply and ship to some port in Great Britain or North Africa certain goods for which they have the agency and which are manufactured in the United States. The goods are shipped from the United States to Canada in packages marked for the place of destination in Canada, and when leaving the United States are assigned to the military forwarding officer at the port of embarkation, and when they reach the port of embarkation the military forwarding officer sees that they are placed on board ship for overseas. Why under such circumstances should the Canadian company go to the custom house and insist on making an entry and paying duty and taxes on these goods?
The question arises, is a racket being worked in connection with such transactions? I do not know, but I should like the minister to give us some explanation of what is actually taking

Supply-Fisheries
place. If there is no racket, why do these Canadian companies insist upon paying these taxes which they are not in the ordinary course of events required to pay? I ask the minister for an explantion of transactions of this kind. If there has been overcharging, steps should be taken to see that the money is refunded and that the guilty persons are punished. I do not know if there has been overcharging or not; but the transactions, it seems to me, are open to question, and I think some explanation is due this committee.

That is very much a matter for the Department of Munitions and Supply to reply to. Normally, when goods are brought into this country for export, if duty is paid at the border when they come in, drawback of the duty is made when the goods are exported. Munitions and supply did, I understand, buy goods on a duty-paid price, and when they came in the duty was paid; when they were exported, whatever duty had been paid would be refundable. Munitions and Supply, when they are now buying goods which are to be exported, buy them and no duty is paid at the border when they come in. The question of cost plus, or profit being made on a duty-paid value, is a matter which came to my attention some time ago and I took it up with the Minister of Munitions and Supply. Of course it is a matter depending on the terms of the contract which the Department of Munitions and Supply make. All we do is collect the duty on the goods which are dutiable, but refund the duty when they are exported.

In this case that has been referred to, as I understand it these people have gone to the customs house and insisted on paying these duties and these taxes. I should like to know why they did that. Why were they so anxious to pay these duties?

Because their contract with the Department of Munitions and Supply called for payment of duty when the goods came in. Munitions and Supply were buying the goods at a duty-paid price and the sellers were to be paid the value of the goods with the duty paid.

I cannot quite understand that either, because there was no duty on them. The goods were clearly marked to be shipped to Great Britain or North Africa or some other place; they were just passing through this country, so that there was no duty on those goods.

Yes, there was. There is a duty on goods coming into this country and
the drawback has to be claimed when goods are exported. Many goods come into this country which we do not know for certain will be exported, and consequently we collect the duty when they come in.

If they are directed to the officer at the port of embarkation, they would come in and pass right through this country to the port, say Saint John, addressed to the officer in charge of embarkation there and marked for shipment overseas. The manifests, as I understand it, must show-at least, I think they would show-the destination of these goods.
As I said before, that system has been changed. If these goods are being shipped overseas and are being sent to a border point, they come in without duty because they are going straight through.
When these refunds were made, to whom were they, made?
They were made to the person paying the duty, but turned over to the Department of Munitions and Supply.
I think I asked the minister in 1942 the total amount of refunds made under such circumstances, and in 1943, up to the end of last month, the total amount.
We would not keep records of that. We keep records, but not of the circumstances of all the refunds made. It would be impossible to give an answer to a question like that.
Has the minister any information whether the breweries are in a position to supply the public with any more beer than they are supplying at the present moment?

A little while ago we did make some arrangements. There was a shortage in the country owing to the oversold condition that existed between October and December when wartime alcoholic beverages came into operation, and arrangements were made to provide the camps and establishments ot all our armed forces with a quota of beer which amounted, I believe, for the remainder of the year to something like two and a half million gallons.

Equally between all the
provinces?

At the rate of a gallon per man per month, wherever he happened to be stationed. We found that the brewers had a great deal of difficulty in providing that. Some of them could not increase their production,

Referring again to the matter I was discussing with the minister, do I understand the minister to say that he cannot tell me the amount of goods that were transmitted to England from the United States for which entry was made and duty paid at the port of Saint John?

We could find it out, but the hon. member asked under the circumstances that they were coming through direct, shipped direct to Saint John for reshipment to Great Britain. I could not possibly give him those figures now. With a great deal of research we could find out what those figures were.

Would it take a great deal of research? By a strange coincidence I happen to have a copy of 'a letter which was written on March 9, 1943. I am going to read it in view of what the minister has said. It came to my hands in a rather strange way.

These are figures which undoubtedly can be procured. But the hon. member is referring to one report.

I know. But for every shipment that goes through a report would go in. These would all have to be collected and tabulated.
